For almost all crypto tokens, the Token Generation Event (TGE) is the best day they will ever have.

For 2026, so far only about 28% of tokens launched remained above their TGE closing price after 60 days. The median token was trading at just 0.64x its launch close.

Tokens surviving and rising in price for days, hours, and even minutes post-launch is not an easy feat. Here are five tokens that have so far avoided the typical post-TGE collapse:

Today, $1WIN is trading around $0.045, roughly 50% above its public sale price.

It is too early to compare that performance with tokens that have been trading for months or years. What makes $1WIN worth paying attention to is that its held steady in the post-TGE price rise and has a big business behind it. 1win has operated since 2016 with 100 million players and its gaming business is profitable independently of the token.

The company also plans revenue-funded open-market buybacks, while 10% of $1WIN spent through supported products will be burned. Supply is capped at one billion tokens with no additional minting.

Hyperliquid’s HYPE remains one of the clearest examples of a token that did considerably more than survive launch.

HYPE began trading in 2024 and today is hitting over $73, leaving it several multiples above its earliest market prices nearly two years later.

The underlying exchange also gives the token an economic connection to platform activity. Trading fees flow into Hyperliquid’s Assistance Fund, which acquires HYPE, with accumulated tokens subsequently burned.

That combination of product usage, revenue and token demand makes HYPE one of the stronger examples of the kind of pre-TGE traction highlighted in Decasonic’s research.

Aster launched ASTER in September 2025 as the token behind its decentralized spot and perpetuals trading platform.

Despite substantial volatility since then, ASTER was trading around $0.65. It remains well below its $2.42 all-time high, but also far above its earliest trading levels.

ASTER has not gone up in a straight line. But more than a year after launch, the token has retained a substantial part of the value created during its early growth rather than fading toward zero after TGE.

Backpack’s BP demonstrates another type of post-TGE resilience.

The token launched in March and subsequently fell as low as roughly $0.12 in May. By this month, BP had recovered to around $0.90, after reaching an all-time high of $1.66 in October.

That makes BP interesting because its strength did not come immediately after TGE. The token went through a deep early correction before rebuilding.

It also sits inside an established exchange and wallet ecosystem, with utility including trading-fee discounts, rewards, staking and access to other Backpack products.

ZAMA is trading around $0.067, approximately one-third above that public auction price.

The token also has direct utility within the Zama Protocol, where it is used to pay for encryption and decryption services and reward operators and stakers securing the network.

Stronger 2026 launches generally arrived with real usage, paying users, revenue, TVL or another measurable source of pre-TGE traction. The token was being added to something that already worked.

A strong launch can be created by hype. Holding up once the launch is over usually requires much more.

#5036. Satoshi-Era Bitcoin Holder Wakes Up After 15 Years, Refuting $250 Billion ‘Lost’ Claim

Disclaimer: The opinions expressed by our writers are their own and do not represent the views of U.Today. The financial and market information provided on U.Today is intended for informational purposes only. U.Today is not liable for any financial losses incurred while trading cryptocurrencies. Conduct your own research by contacting financial experts before making any investment decisions. We believe that all content is accurate as of the date of publication, but certain offers mentioned may no longer be available.

A Bitcoin address that had not moved coins since February 2011 transferred 75 BTC on Nov. 17, according to Galaxy Research. At the current price of $64,935 per BTC, the coins are worth around $4.87 million.

The address is listed as a defendant in a $250 billion lawsuit in New York Supreme Court, in which the plaintiffs are trying to have early Bitcoin wallets declared "lost." Galaxy Research said that several other addresses from the same list have also moved coins in 2026.

According to Galaxy Research analysts, early on Nov. 17, in block 976,209, the address 1ALpEWtXApR19hLXvcG8NfkPyGsUMhFPMS sent coins for the first time. It was first funded on Feb. 8, 2011. At that time, Bitcoin was trading at about $0.90. After 15.8 years, the coins went to an unknown address with a 399-satoshi fee, or about 26 cents, for a paper gain of more than 7,000,000%.

Onchain databases list the wallet as Noah Doe #3409 (Salomon Client Dusted). That label is how it ended up among the defendants in the high-profile case ABC Company, XYZ Company, and Noah Doe v. John Does 1–39,069.

According to the lawsuit, an anonymous plaintiff using the pseudonym Noah Doe and two companies want the rights to 39,069 Bitcoin wallets that have not moved coins for more than five years. The plaintiffs said that these wallets hold about 3.8 million BTC, and at the current price, the coins are worth around $250 billion.

The plaintiffs filed the lawsuit under New York's lost-and-found law, Article 7-B of the Personal Property Law. Under the law, a person who finds lost property has to give it to the police, and the property goes to the finder if the owner does not claim it in time. In the lawsuit, the plaintiffs valued each address at less than $10, and they argued that the waiting period for such items was one year.

They "found" dormant addresses with an algorithm, saved them onto USB flash drives and took them to the New York Police Department (NYPD). Then they served the owners on the blockchain, through microtransactions with embedded messages (OP_RETURN). The practice is known as "dusting," and the campaign is tied to Salomon Brothers Strategic Advisors. Once the waiting period ran out, the plaintiffs asked the court to recognize the coins as theirs.

The case has been put on hold several times over motions to dismiss and amicus curiae briefs from outside experts. At a hearing on Sept. 8, the Bitcoin Policy Institute asked to intervene as a defendant, and The Digital Chamber asked to join the case as amicus curiae. Galaxy Research described it as a case "in which anonymous plaintiffs are seeking to claim legal title over Satoshi's coins."

Galaxy Research's Will Owens, who attended the hearing, said that The Digital Chamber's arguments were "well pleaded" and that "the judge sounded sympathetic to them."

Critics of the lawsuit argue that Article 7-B was written for things you can pick up and hand over for safekeeping. It wasn't written for blockchain records when the "finder" doesn't hold the private keys.

In September, Galaxy head of research Alex Thorn also said that the Lost and Found Property Law includes "protection from 'Noah Doe-style' dormancy attacks on legal ownership."

#5035. 'Nobody Knows Who's in Charge': Boris Johnson Stands by Bitcoin Skepticism at Breakpoint

'Nobody Knows Who's in Charge': Boris Johnson Stands by Bitcoin Skepticism at Breakpoint

Former UK Prime Minister Boris Johnson is sticking to his doubts about Bitcoin, telling a room full of crypto developers that he still can't see who is in charge of the world's largest cryptocurrency.

"As far as I can see, nobody knows who's in charge, apart from Yakimoto Nakasori, and I don't know where to find him," Johnson said at Solana's Breakpoint conference in London, deliberately mangling the name of Bitcoin's pseudonymous creator, Satoshi Nakamoto. "If six billion got stolen from some cryptocurrency, I wouldn't know who to apply to, or how to get the money back. That's my problem."

Johnson was asked about a column he wrote in March for the Daily Mail, in which he called Bitcoin a "giant Ponzi scheme." The column drew pushback from the crypto industry, including Strategy executive chairman Michael Saylor, who tweeted that Bitcoin has no issuer, promoter or guaranteed return.

Bitcoin is not a Ponzi scheme. A Ponzi requires a central operator promising returns and paying early investors with funds from later ones. Bitcoin has no issuer, no promoter, and no guaranteed return—just an open, decentralized monetary network driven by code and market demand.

— Michael Saylor (@saylor) March 13, 2026

On stage, Johnson admitted he is "not a great crypto buff" and holds little, if any, crypto himself. His view was shaped by a man he met in his Oxfordshire village who had lost thousands and kept paying more in the hope of recovering his losses, he said. "If the search for the greater fool had reached the wilds of South Oxfordshire, then probably there was something not quite right about this thing," Johnson said.

He also questioned the name itself, noting that "crypto" comes from the Greek for "hidden." "I don't think it's a good sell to tell people that this thing is concealed," he said.

Johnson drew a sharp line between Bitcoin and the technology behind it. "Please don't think that my Luddite anxiety about crypto in any way means that I wish to slow down the development of blockchain, or the lead that London should rightly have in that sort of technology," he said. When it comes to blockchain and tokenizing assets, the UK has "got to be at the forefront," he added.

Moderator Gareth Jenkinson, head of multimedia at The Block, pushed back when Johnson suggested Bitcoin was valuable to drug dealers, arguing that blockchains are far more traceable than cash. Asked by Johnson who guarantees Bitcoin, Jenkinson replied: "No one has to guarantee it. That's the beauty of the protocol."

Lord Ross Kempsell, a Conservative member of the House of Lords who previously worked for Johnson, said more than 8% of UK adults now hold some form of crypto asset, and that institutional adoption of blockchains is growing in the City of London. That ownership figure has fallen, however: the Financial Conduct Authority's latest consumer research, conducted in August and September 2025, found 8% of UK adults own crypto, down from 12% in 2024, though still double the level in 2021.

The UK is "on the precipice of creating a lot of regulation" for the sector, Kempsell said, pointing to the FCA's work on its regulatory perimeter and the Bank of England's coming stablecoin framework. "I share Boris's anxieties about the risks," he said, but within that perimeter, "there's a lot of scope here for a high growth industry."

In June, the FCA finalized its rulebook for crypto firms ahead of a mandatory regime due to take effect in late 2027, days after the Bank of England eased its stablecoin rules, scrapping planned individual holding caps in favor of a £40 billion issuance limit per coin. The Bank has since been handed a legal duty to foster stablecoin innovation, and it has set out a shared vision for tokenization with the FCA.

Kempsell also argued that being outside the EU's Markets in Crypto-Assets (MiCA) regulation allows the UK to set its own rules for crypto. The EU itself is set to revise MiCA in 2027 to cover foreign stablecoin issuers.

#5032. Ripple-Backed Evernorth Takes Massive $505 Million XRP Hit

Ripple-backed XRP treasury company Evernorth Holdings has disclosed a significant decrease in the book value of its crypto asset holdings, with total impairment charges amounting to around $505 million before going public on Nasdaq.

Per an SEC filing on Nov. 13, the 346.3 million XRP tokens that Evernorth Holdings owned had a book value of just $341.9 million as of Sept. 30, 2026.

This is compared to the firm's initial accounting of the crypto assets at roughly $846.6 million, with an average acquisition or contribution price of $2.44 per XRP. This represents a nearly 60% decline in book value.

As per the latest filing, Evernorth recorded around $271 million in XRP impairment charges in the first nine months of 2026. This is in addition to the $233.7 million in impairment charges recorded in 2025.

Interestingly, only $6.9 million of the recent impairment charges occurred in the third quarter.

This also explains why Evernorth's XRP assets had a book value so far below their market value at the end of September.

Evernorth calculates impairments based on the lowest observable intraday price of XRP for each batch of tokens acquired. Once the assets are written down, the company is unable to reverse the previous losses if the price rises.

For reference, on Sept. 30, XRP closed the day trading at around $1.49 on Coinbase. At that price, Evernorth's 346.3 million XRP tokens would have been worth roughly $516 million, much higher than the disclosed book value of $341.9 million.

The recent disclosure comes around a month after Evernorth completed its business combination with Armada Acquisition Corp. II on Oct. 9. It started trading on Nasdaq under the symbol XRPN on Oct. 12.

Following the business combination, Evernorth held around 473 million XRP tokens and had also raised gross cash proceeds of around $300 million.

Its investors include Ripple, SBI Group, Arrington Capital, Pantera Capital, Kraken and GSR.

On Oct. 14, Evernorth announced collaborations with Ripple, Kraken, Coinbase and BitGo to implement institutional investment strategies starting in Q4 2026.

Meanwhile, its latest SEC filing did not include details on the amount of XRP deployed to generate yield or the returns generated from it.

#5031. Google uncovers AI hacking tool that turns security fixes into cyberattacks

Researchers discovered an attacker-controlled system capable of identifying software vulnerabilities, generating exploits and executing attacks automatically.

Google has uncovered an AI-powered hacking system capable of transforming software security fixes into automated attacks against vulnerable websites.

In a Nov. 16 report, Google Threat Intelligence Group and Mandiant revealed that attackers were using AI frameworks to identify vulnerabilities, generate malicious code, and execute exploits with minimal human involvement.

The researchers discovered one such system, dubbed exploit_agent, on an exposed staging server containing multiple AI models connected to cybersecurity research and exploitation tools.

The framework was configured to monitor software updates, compare patched code with older versions, and identify weaknesses that developers had recently repaired. It could subsequently generate attack code and execute it automatically, allowing attackers to target websites that had not yet installed the relevant security updates.

This approach exploits the information developers publish when addressing software vulnerabilities. Changes made to repair a flaw can inadvertently reveal how the underlying weakness could be exploited.

Google said the technique lets attackers focus on known vulnerabilities rather than spend time discovering previously unknown security flaws.

The company's investigation also uncovered stolen victim data and malicious scripts capable of conducting internal network reconnaissance, brute-force attacks and installing webshells that provide remote access to compromised servers.

Some tools could remove webshells left by competing attackers, potentially helping the operator retain control over compromised systems.

Google found evidence that the operator was particularly interested in French websites associated with media, entertainment, and education. One recovered example showed the framework examining access-control protections in Spectra, a WordPress plugin used for website development.

Google describes exploit_agent comparing patched code, identifying potential weaknesses, drafting exploits and executing them automatically.

A published fix can guide attack development while website owners are still deploying the update.

The diagram shows Google's configured pipeline, not measured timing, a success rate or proof of an entirely autonomous campaign.

Conceptual process diagram of Google's configured exploit_agent pipeline. Arrows encode sequence and input flow, not elapsed time, conversion rate or successful compromise.

The diagram shows Google's configured pipeline, not measured timing, a success rate or proof of an entirely autonomous campaign.

The discovery marked the first time Google had identified attackers using AI frameworks to fully automate vulnerability discovery and exploitation without human intervention throughout the process.

Thanks for signing up to The Catalyst. Look out for your first daily email. If you already receive it, you’re all set.

Google's report also revealed a separate campaign in which suspected North Korean hackers exploited AI-powered development tools to infiltrate cryptocurrency organizations in North America and Europe.

The attackers, tracked as MIDNIGHT NEPTUNE, combined AI-generated identities with fraudulent recruitment campaigns to gain access to corporate systems.

They created fake recruiter profiles on professional networking platforms using AI-generated photographs, then directed prospective victims to fraudulent meeting websites.

Those websites instructed victims to run supposed troubleshooting commands that instead executed malicious scripts.

Once inside an organization, the attackers accessed internal code repositories and modified configuration files used by Anthropic's Claude Code development assistant.

The altered files were designed to automatically download a backdoor known as SOMBERMEME whenever employees launched Claude Code.

Google also discovered that the attackers disguised GitHub access tokens using names associated with Microsoft Copilot, concealing their movements within compromised development environments.

The campaign expanded on North Korea's established use of AI to generate fake resumes, prepare for job interviews, and impersonate Western technology workers seeking remote employment.

Google said the latest intrusions showed how attackers exploited AI development tools already embedded in corporate workflows to distribute malicious software.

Meanwhile, the emergence of autonomous exploitation frameworks threatens to accelerate attacks against organizations running outdated software.

Google warned that automating vulnerability analysis and exploit execution could substantially reduce the time between disclosing a security flaw and exploiting it, leaving website operators with increasingly narrow windows to install protective updates.

#5030. DTCC, Barclays Say Tokenization's Real Prize Is Unlocking Idle Collateral

DTCC, Barclays Say Tokenization's Real Prize Is Unlocking Idle Collateral

The biggest payoff from tokenizing traditional assets won't come from simply putting them onchain, but from putting idle collateral to work, according to executives at the Depository Trust & Clearing Corporation (DTCC) and Barclays.

"You can tokenize an asset, but if you can't do anything with it, what's the point?" Val Wooton, DTCC's global head of equities solutions, said at Solana's Breakpoint conference in London. "For me, it really is around collateral and liquidity."

Scott Lucas, head of digital assets at Barclays, agreed. A lot of collateral sits "relatively idle" at central securities depositories, he said, and much of the early value for banks will come from moving it more efficiently between their own accounts, before extending that to clients. "There's a lot of money in good housekeeping," he added.

The pair spoke on a panel days after DTCC announced that its tokenization service will connect to Solana, with tokenized assets expected on the network in the second half of 2027.

The service, which launched on October 28, can tokenize assets held at DTCC's depository, starting with Russell 1000 stocks, ETFs tracking major indexes, and U.S. Treasury bills and bonds, Wooton said. The tokens carry the same legal and economic rights as traditionally held securities, and adding Solana reflects DTCC's strategy of being "open," "interoperable" and "multi-network," he added.

Wooton said the biggest opportunity lies in "liquidity optimization," which he said could save "millions, if not billions" of dollars by letting firms move assets that are currently stuck when markets are closed.

Large financial institutions today over-fund and over-collateralize every day because they treat collateral as "just in case," he said. Moving assets onchain, around the clock, would let firms manage collateral "just in time," freeing up "a significant amount of balance sheet" to put to other uses. He added that the ability to move assets and settle them atomically could be "extremely powerful" in times of market stress.

Lucas pointed to Barclays' participation in DTCC's tokenization launch last month, one of the bank's first public moves into the space, and described the efficiency gains from managing its own collateral as good housekeeping.

Barclays is also working with Ironlight on tokenized structured products, Lucas said, though he stressed "it's not a done deal." He added that he would like to see Solana adopted by other central securities depositories around the world, building a shared infrastructure layer across Asia-Pacific, Europe and the United States.

Both executives said adoption remains early. Wooton said the industry is "still in the crawl stage," and that traditional and digital rails will exist side by side "for quite a long time," though DTCC's clients are already tokenizing assets daily.

Lucas said he tries to stay "healthily skeptical" about the speed of adoption while making sure Barclays is ready for its clients. At a recent traditional finance conference in Miami, he said, "every institution we met had money on the table," making investments and building products, a shift from a year earlier, when most were still asking questions.

Barclays has been gradually expanding its crypto activities. The bank invested in U.S. stablecoin startup Ubyx earlier this year and has reportedly weighed a push into tokenized deposits and stablecoin payments, according to Bloomberg. It was also among the investors backing crypto custodian Copper in 2022.

Bank of America held 13,000 shares of the fund in the first quarter and 13,260 shares in the second quarter, according to its earlier 13F filings. The same filing lists more than $685 million in BlackRock's IBIT, $13.58 million in Bitwise and $950,000 in VanEck.

Seven major banks disclosed XRP fund holdings worth a total of $29.4 million in filings published between Nov. 9 and Nov. 16. #5028. Bitcoin Lightning developers needed two patches to stop a potentially costly attack

The initial July update blocked one crash method but missed a persistent vulnerability that could leave affected nodes unable to restart.

Bitcoin's Core Lightning software required two security patches to eliminate a vulnerability that could repeatedly crash payment nodes and potentially expose funds held in other channels.

A Nov. 13 security disclosure revealed that an initial repair released in July failed to address a second attack method that could keep affected nodes offline even after they restarted.

The vulnerability, tracked as LNF-2026-0004, affected Core Lightning, one of the software implementations used to operate nodes on Bitcoin's Lightning Network.

Security researcher Nishant Bansal discovered that attackers could exploit how Core Lightning assigned identifiers to payment channels, creating duplicate records that caused the software to crash.

The weakness originated in the network's channel-opening process, where each payment channel receives an identifier derived from the Bitcoin transaction output that funds it. Core Lightning could accept multiple channels referencing the same funding output, producing identical identifiers that conflicted with assumptions in its internal software.

In the first attack, a malicious peer could create duplicate pending channels and crash a victim's node simply by reconnecting. The attack required no Bitcoin transaction fees because the fraudulent channels did not need on-chain funding. Each subsequent reconnection could trigger another crash, allowing attackers to repeatedly interrupt payment processing.

However, researchers identified a more persistent variation involving previously closed channels.

By reusing an identifier associated with a closed channel and subsequently closing another channel with the same identifier, attackers could trigger a software failure that persisted across restarts.

Unlike the initial attack, this method required on-chain transaction fees but could leave the node unable to recover without a software upgrade.

Core Lightning developers addressed the original vulnerability in version 26.06.6, released on July 22, after researchers privately reported the reconnection attack earlier that month.

The update prevented new channels from reusing funding outputs associated with existing live channels. It also modified connection handling to prevent duplicate records already stored from triggering the original crash.

However, the protection did not extend to identifiers associated with closed channels, leaving the second attack route available.

Researcher Crypt-iQ independently identified the remaining weakness, prompting developers to introduce broader safeguards in version 26.06.8, released Sept. 22.

The second update expanded duplicate-identifier checks across active and closed channels belonging to different peers. It also allowed nodes containing previously stored duplicate records to recover without repeatedly crashing.

July’s repair checked live channels. September’s also covered closed channels and allowed recovery from duplicates already stored.

The first fix blocked outpoints reused among that peer’s live channels and handled reconnect duplicates. Closed-channel collisions could still cause a persistent restart loop.

The broader fix rejected IDs used by live or closed channels across all peers and let nodes load and close duplicates already stored.

Operators should upgrade to the latest release to prevent collisions and handle stored duplicates.

The closed-channel loop shown is the documented persistent path; a separate free nonpersistent path also existed. This qualitative schematic does not show exploitation, losses or affected-node counts.

Qualitative schematic of the common collision mechanism and two historical patch scopes. Toggle compares July 22 v26.06.6 with September 22 v26.06.8. Connectors show software paths, not counts, timing or money flows.

The closed-channel loop shown is the documented persistent path; a separate free nonpersistent path also existed. This qualitative schematic does not show exploitation, losses or affected-node counts.

The potential financial consequences extended beyond disrupted Lightning payments.

According to the advisory, nodes forced offline could lose the ability to monitor Bitcoin's blockchain for attempts to settle channels using revoked transaction states.

That could allow dishonest counterparties to claim funds using outdated channel balances. Offline nodes could also miss deadlines for collecting time-sensitive payments, placing Bitcoin held in unrelated channels at risk.

The researchers did not report confirmed exploitation or financial losses.

The findings affect Core Lightning versions preceding the complete September repair, with the reconnection vulnerability dating back to version 0.12.0 and the persistent closed-channel crash introduced in version 25.05.

Developers have since released additional security updates, including version 26.06.10, which addresses other vulnerabilities involving channel operations, payment resolution, and remote crashes.

Core Lightning's maintainers have urged operators to upgrade to the latest release to protect their nodes against the disclosed weaknesses.

#5027. XRP’s 10-Year RSI Low Fuels Debate Over a Bottom

Home » Trendsetter News » XRP’s 10-Year RSI Low Fuels Debate Over a Bottom

Analysts see possible recovery signals, but extreme oversold conditions don’t confirm a reversal: further deficit remains possible.

XRP’s daily relative strength index has fallen to its lowest reading since 2016, according to chart analysis cited by Matt, the cryptocurrency YouTuber presenting the new Moon Lambo video episode.

His central argument: extreme selling pressure may signal an opportunity, even as XRP price trades below $1 and investors remain deeply fearful.

In the recording, dated November 17, 2026, Matt puts XRP just below $0.96 and Bitcoin at $64,571. He also cites a Crypto Fear and Greed Index reading of 12 out of 100, firmly in “extreme fear” territory. Those figures are presented in the video rather than independently verified market data.

The most striking figure comes from Crypto Insight UK: an XRP daily RSI of 16.17, described as its lowest in a decade. Matt acknowledges the limitation directly: “Just because we’re oversold doesn’t mean we can’t go lower.”

The weekly chart offers a less straightforward signal. Citing analyst D Greg Crypto, Matt describes XRP’s weekly RSI falling below 20, recovering that level and then quickly testing it again—an unusually compressed sequence compared with previous recoveries.

Under that analysis, holding above 20 could support a potential double-bottom momentum structure. A sustained break below it would instead leave room for further capitulation. The distinction matters: an extreme indicator reading is not the same thing as a confirmed price bottom.

Matt also highlights Charting Guy’s view that XRP resembles a previous cycle’s bottoming process, with a weekly bullish divergence and a possible re-accumulation pattern. That analyst maintains a minimum xrp price target of $4.36, not a forecast for the eventual peak.

The timing is considerably less certain. Charting Guy suggests possible altcoin seasons in summer 2027 and late 2028, while Matt argues that Bitcoin’s direction will remain important for XRP and the wider market.

Matt’s own response is to keep holding rather than trade the volatility. He identifies himself as an enthusiast without a financial background, not a financial adviser.

For now, the consequential question is whether exhausted selling develops into sustained buying. Moon Lambo presents several arguments for recovery, but its own weekly-RSI discussion leaves a clear risk unresolved: XRP price could remain under pressure before any broader market rebound takes hold.

#5026. Binance hack may push institutions to outside custody, FalconX exec says

FalconX’s Joshua Lim says the Binance hack could push institutions to keep crypto off exchanges and change how large investors trade in 2027.

A major shift in institutional crypto trading could be on the horizon following the recent Binance hack, as security concerns may lead to more large investors keeping their assets outside exchanges, according to a FalconX executive.

In an exclusive interview with Cointelegraph at the Digital Asset Forum in New York City on Nov. 13, Joshua Lim, global head of markets at FalconX, a digital asset brokerage for institutional investors, said the Oct. 29 hack could make institutions more cautious about trading crypto and change how they store their assets.

“It’s actually quite bearish for more institutional participation in crypto,” Lim told Cointelegraph. He said traders initially played down the hack but later began to recognize its potential long-term impact.

As a result, Lim expects more institutions to turn to outside custody providers and trading firms that allow them to trade without keeping their crypto on exchanges, a shift he believes could become one of the biggest trends in 2027.

North Korean-linked hackers stole about $6.4 billion in cryptocurrency from Binance, making it the largest crypto theft on record, according to blockchain analytics firm Chainalysis.

The shift toward keeping crypto outside exchanges already appeared to be underway even before the hack. In an October proposal, the US Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) said industry practices were developing that reduced the need to move investment advisers’ client assets and regulated funds’ crypto holdings out of permitted custody for trading.

Lim pointed to Copper, a crypto custody provider, as one company that could benefit. Its ClearLoop service lets investors trade on supported exchanges while keeping their crypto with a separate company.

Copper said collateral protected by its ClearLoop service supported more than $240 billion in perpetual futures trading volume during the first quarter of 2026, more than double the amount a year earlier.

Lim explained that investors can keep their assets outside an exchange while receiving credited balances that allow them to trade on it. Under the brokerage model Lim described, a hedge fund can place trades through FalconX, which executes them using its own exchange accounts and relationships. Still, investors face risks tied to the firms holding their assets and settling their trades.

“For many players, facing a regulated entity like ours is more palatable,” Lim added.

Related: Crypto hack losses equal 57 cents per $1 earned onchain: Ark’s Valente

Binance recorded large Bitcoin outflows in mid-November, although it is not clear whether they were linked to the hack.

According to CryptoQuant data, Binance recorded net withdrawals of about 2,771 Bitcoin (BTC) on Friday, followed by 2,708 BTC on Saturday and 5,636 BTC on Sunday — totaling about 11,115 BTC leaving the exchange than entered over those three days.

The withdrawals came as the broader crypto market was falling, with Bitcoin trading around $65,000 at 9:41 pm UTC Monday, down about 20% over the past month, according to CoinGecko.

However, the data does not show who moved the Bitcoin or why. Investors could have transferred their funds to personal wallets, companies that store crypto on their behalf, or to other exchanges.

Beyond concerns about exchange security, Lim expects other changes in how large investors trade in 2027. He said institutions want more ways to trade assets such as oil, gold and stock market indexes through crypto platforms, including outside regular market hours.

“You can respond quickly to news events when they happen,” Lim said, citing one of the benefits of 24/7 trading.

That type of trading is already taking place on Hyperliquid, a decentralized trading platform that offers contracts tied to traditional assets. As of Monday, Hyperliquid’s markets for traditional assets and other contracts had about $4.3 billion in open interest and recorded $3.9 billion in trading volume over 24 hours, according to data from Perpys.

But while crypto platforms are giving investors more ways to trade, Lim said the financial services needed to support those trades have not kept up, particularly when it comes to borrowing money and managing risk.

For example, investors can now trade oil through traditional futures markets, investment funds and crypto platforms. But lenders may treat trades on each platform separately, even when those trades balance each other out.

“There’s not enough players that can give you leverage or margin financing against all of these things collectively,” Lim said. “The risk netting is not quite there yet.”

#5025. Bitcoin's $90,000 Comeback Now Unlikely, Novogratz Warns

Galaxy Digital CEO Mike Novogratz said that the odds of Bitcoin hitting $90,000 by the end of 2026 are slim in light of prevailing macroeconomic headwinds and the growing likelihood that the Federal Reserve may hike interest rates.

During a live event with Anthony Scaramucci at the Digital Assets Forum in New York City, Novogratz was asked if Bitcoin could get back to $90,000 by the end of this year.

"Less likely than it was. You need something to happen," Novogratz said.

His gloomy outlook comes as Bitcoin has struggled to rebound after a devastating drop that saw its price dip as low as $62,000 over the weekend. Bitcoin's price stood at around $64,600 on Nov. 17. The largest cryptocurrency by market capitalization has declined for six consecutive weeks.

A shift in the U.S. monetary policy outlook, namely the prospect of more rate hikes from the Federal Reserve, has been largely to blame for Bitcoin's decline, according to Novogratz.

"At the start of the year, everybody thought the Fed was going to be cutting now," he said.

But high inflation and ongoing supply shocks have forced investors to readjust their expectations.

"Inflation's going up. We've got inflation going up," Novogratz said, warning that inflationary pressures could become increasingly entrenched.

"The Fed's going to hike. At least two more, probably three more," he said.

Novogratz predicted that the Fed would raise rates by 25 basis points in December and then hike again at its next meeting.

He said that higher rates, at least in the near term, tend to weigh on Bitcoin. But the higher cost of government borrowing could eventually provide support for the cryptocurrency.

"Yeah, later," he said in response to the suggestion that higher borrowing costs could be a tailwind for Bitcoin.

"First, you're gonna hike rates. Oh, sell gold, right? You're going to go to the dollar. It's so ingrained in peoples' heads," he said.

"Carry costs going up," he said. Bitcoin doesn't offer the same yield as interest-bearing dollar assets.

"You don't make any interest on Bitcoin in dollars," he said.

In particular, Novogratz said that the massive rise in Treasury yields has been particularly detrimental to the crypto market.

"Literally 40 basis points in like four days of trading. So that's why crypto's down," he said.

He also said that the massive crypto hack could still be weighing on investors' minds, adding to market jitters.

"I think in the back of their minds is the hack," he said.

#5024. Solana Drops 'Mainnet Beta' After Six Years: Here's What 1.0 Is All About

Solana Drops 'Mainnet Beta' After Six Years: Here's What 1.0 Is All About

Solana is officially out of beta, more than six years after launching a blockchain that has been handling real money the whole time.

The Solana Foundation on Monday retired the “mainnet beta” label and introduced Solana 1.0, a shared version number for the network's underlying rules. The change is primarily about how developers and validator operators coordinate software updates, not a fresh boost to transaction speed or any other meaningful improvement over what users already have.

Solana launched its mainnet beta on March 16, 2020, and kept the experimental-sounding name even as users traded tokens, built applications, and moved assets across the chain.

Nothing happens to those assets now. “Your SOL, accounts, assets, applications, and transaction history remain the same,” the Foundation said. Users don't need to swap tokens, move wallets or install anything to keep using the network.

Solana has two major validator clients: Agave, developed by Anza, and Firedancer, built independently by Jump Crypto. Each has its own code, release schedule and version numbers, which can make it harder to tell whether different software releases support the same network features.

Solana 1.0 creates a common reference point for the protocol itself. An Agave release and a Firedancer release can support the same protocol version without sharing a software version number.

That distinction matters as the network relies on more than one software implementation. A bug in one client need not affect every validator, although software diversity alone cannot guarantee the network will stay online.

“Announcing a protocol version does not activate every associated improvement at once,” the Foundation warned. Operators still need to check whether their particular software supports a planned upgrade and follow its activation instructions.

The Foundation said it coordinated the change with Anza and the Firedancer team. Its announcement does not describe a new voting system or a change in who governs Solana; the network's governance process for proposals remains separate.

The Foundation credits engineering work that preceded Monday's announcement, particularly Alpenglow and Firedancer. Solana's Alpenglow upgrade went live on October 21, replacing the system validators had used to reach agreement since launch.

Alpenglow targets transaction finality of roughly 150 milliseconds, compared with about 12.8 seconds previously. Finality is the point at which a transaction is considered settled; that improvement came from the October upgrade, not from calling the network 1.0.

Firedancer also reached mainnet in 2025, giving validators a separately developed alternative to Agave. That reduces dependence on a single codebase, though the extent of the protection depends on how widely different clients are actually used.

Solana has reasons to be careful with promises of reliability. Its network went offline for nearly five hours in February 2024, following an outage lasting almost 19 hours a year earlier.

Documentation and block explorers will gradually adopt the new mainnet name, according to the Foundation. Its upgrade tracker still lists Agave 4.4 as planned for November and Agave 4.5 for December, each with its own release and activation requirements.

#5023. Bitcoin developer verifies 164 million unspent coins in just 72 seconds

An experimental cryptographic system could dramatically reduce Bitcoin node setup times by replacing extensive historical checks with compact mathematical proofs.

A Bitcoin developer has shown how to verify a 9.39 GB blockchain snapshot in just 72 seconds, potentially making it easier and faster to run Bitcoin nodes.

The developer, identified as l-henri, disclosed the experiment in a Nov. 13 Delving Bitcoin post, describing a system that uses cryptographic proofs to check Bitcoin's existing transaction records without independently processing its entire history.

The experiment involved a snapshot containing approximately 164.5 million unspent transaction outputs (UTXOs) at Bitcoin block 972,500. These outputs represent Bitcoin that has been received but not yet spent, forming the database nodes use to determine whether coins remain available for transactions.

Using an arm64 computer with approximately 0.5 GB of memory, the developer checked that the snapshot matched the records established by a cryptographic proof.

The process took approximately 72 seconds, with nearly all that time spent reading the 9.39 GB file. Separately, the developer demonstrated that a compact 1.6 MB proof could be verified in a web browser in about half a second.

The achievement could help address a practical challenge of running Bitcoin infrastructure: the time and computing resources required to verify historical blockchain activity before a node becomes fully operational.

Bitcoin nodes help secure the network by independently checking transactions and enforcing its rules.

Traditionally, setting up a fully validating node involves downloading and processing BTC's historical transactions to reconstruct the current database of spendable coins.

Bitcoin Core already offers a shortcut through a feature called assumeUTXO, which lets nodes start operating using a snapshot of the blockchain's transaction state. However, the software continues verifying historical transactions in the background to confirm that the snapshot accurately reflects Bitcoin's records.

L-henri's experiment proposes replacing that additional verification work with a cryptographic proof. This approach could let new nodes accept a verified snapshot without repeating extensive historical calculations, potentially reducing setup time and resource requirements.

The developer's system uses STARK proofs, which allow computers to verify specified calculations without repeating every step themselves. In this experiment, the proof covered BTC's block headers from its beginning and checked changes to unspent coins between blocks 935,001 and 972,500.

However, the calculations started from an existing trusted Bitcoin Core snapshot at block 935,000 rather than rebuilding the entire transaction history. The system also excluded checks of transaction scripts and signatures, meaning it does not yet provide the same verification guarantees as a fully validating BTC node.

These limitations remain important as the developer considers integrating the technology into Bitcoin Core.

In the November disclosure, l-henri proposed testing a modification that would let Bitcoin Core accept proof-backed snapshots and skip its existing background validation process.

That would mark a departure from Bitcoin Core's current approach, which independently checks historical records even after loading a snapshot.

The project remains experimental and has not undergone an external security review. Bitcoin Core also does not currently support the proposed integration.

The next step is to test whether the proof system can provide sufficient verification guarantees to replace historical checks without weakening the security assumptions BTC nodes rely on.

#5022. Hoskinson: Cardano Not Done Yet

Charles Hoskinson made sure to clear up misunderstandings about whether he thought the work on Cardano was done.

"I never once said Cardano is finished," Hoskinson said in a Nov. 15 post on X.

The comments came after he talked about the completion of Cardano's original roadmap, which raised some questions about his role in the blockchain's future.

He also called out the CEO of the Cardano Foundation, Frederik Gregaard, for not mentioning the Midnight chain when discussing everything the network has accomplished.

In his latest video, uploaded on Nov. 17, Hoskinson celebrated the fact that Midnight had just brought on board its first UK-based banking partner, Monument Bank.

Monument Bank is the first UK bank to offer interest-bearing tokenized retail deposits on a public blockchain, according to an announcement from the Midnight Foundation.

Up to £250 million in customer deposits will be added to Midnight in the first phase, and each tokenized deposit will be backed 1:1 by sterling cash held at the bank.

Monument Bank customers can now earn a fixed 5.2% annual equivalent rate on deposits for 12 months, all without having to deal with cryptocurrencies directly.

Hoskinson was very excited about the scale of the initiative, comparing the planned amount of deposits with the current decentralized finance ecosystem on Cardano.

"It's five times the TVL of Cardano," he said.

The £250 million is the planned initial size of the banking product, not a verified figure for how much is currently deposited on Midnight.

Hoskinson called this one of the most important milestones in his career.

"This is just one of the many things to come, but I think it's one of the most significant things of at least my career," he said.

He added that the team behind Midnight had moved the originally scheduled hard fork from December to November to accommodate the technical needs of Monument Bank.

Despite the milestone, Hoskinson emphasized that it's only the first step in a much larger mission: bringing traditional financial assets onto Midnight.

Hoskinson thinks the main barrier to cryptocurrency adoption is the lack of trust among consumers. He believes that simplifying the user experience without compromising regulatory requirements will allow billions of people to join the blockchain economy.

Hoskinson also shared that there's a big event coming up for the Midnight Foundation on Dec. 15. Developers will showcase future products and technological advancements scheduled for 2027.

#5021. Ripple CTO Emeritus Reveals Why XRP Took BTC’s Code

Home » Ripple (XRP) » Ripple CTO Emeritus Reveals Why XRP Took BTC’s Code

Here’s why XRP’s Ledger still supports the original elliptic curve that Bitcoin uses for signatures.

David Schwartz, Ripple’s CTO Emeritus and one of the original architects of the XRP Ledger, explained a deliberate early design choice this week.

Responding to a post about the ledger’s technical roots, he wrote: “We did things that way in the very early days because we didn’t want to face potential criticism that our choices of those core crypto functions were less secure than bitcoin’s.”

The discussion began with XRPL validator Vet, who noted that the ledger’s earliest code included helper functions and comments from Bitcoin’s original client, written by Satoshi Nakamoto and copied by early developer Jed McCaleb.

Did you know all of us on the XRP Ledger use design choices by Satoshi daily?15 years ago, the XRP Ledger started out using some Bitcoin code, including helper functions from the Bitcoin client that Satoshi wrote.Jed copied Satoshi's timekeeping code into the XRPL, including… pic.twitter.com/IZOaa4w0bz

Most of that code was removed by the end of 2014; in December of that year, then-engineering lead Nik Bougalis deleted the last of the timekeeping routines along with one of Satoshi’s comments.

Two design choices remain. The XRP Ledger still supports the secp256k1 elliptic curve that Bitcoin uses for signatures (it also supports the newer Ed25519 curve, so not every account relies on secp256k1).

Separately, every XRPL address is still generated the Bitcoin way: the public key is hashed with SHA-256 and then with RIPEMD-160 before encoding. Those steps are used by every account on the network today.

David Schwartz’s explanation is straightforward. In the network’s first years, the team preferred to reuse cryptographic primitives already proven in Bitcoin rather than introduce untested alternatives that crypto critics, particularly in the Bitcoin community, could attack as weaker or experimental.

We did things that way in the very early days because we didn't want to face potential criticism that our choices of those core crypto functions were less secure than bitcoin's.

Using the same curve and address-generation method removed one potential line of criticism before it could be raised. Ripple CTO Emeritus has noted it is impossible to know whether different choices would actually have drawn that criticism; the point was to avoid having to defend the cryptography at all.

The early code sharing was limited and temporary. The consensus mechanism, transaction model, and most of the ledger’s architecture were built independently.

It's hard to say. Obviously, we never got those criticisms. But it's hard to know if we would have. I'm not sure we would have come up with better ones had we made our own decisions anyway.

What survived are two well-understood cryptographic building blocks that have remained secure and widely implemented for more than a decade. Later additions, including Ed25519 support, gave users and developers additional options without removing the original path.

The exchange is a small window into how the XRP Ledger was constructed: deliberately conservative on core cryptography in its first years, then gradually cleaned of borrowed code once the project had its footing. The two pieces are still in daily use by everyone on-chain.

#5020. BlackRock holds 123,056 Strategy shares ahead of MSCI exit, but how much must it sell?

Three BlackRock ETFs reported 123,056 Strategy shares ahead of MSCI's Nov. 30 removal, raising questions about selling pressure.

When you buy an index fund, you're paying a manager to follow a particular group of stocks. MSCI creates these indexes and sets their membership rules, while companies such as BlackRock manage the funds that follow them.

MSCI is removing Strategy from several of its indexes after Nov. 30. Funds following those indexes will then be trying to match the performance of a group that no longer includes Michael Saylor's Bitcoin-buying company.

It's easy to see why investors expect selling: a fund that bought Strategy to follow an index loses that reason to own it when the stock drops out. But two BlackRock funds tracking the same MSCI index show why we can't simply add up all their investments and treat the total as a sell order.

One owns thousands of Strategy shares, while the other uses contracts with financial institutions to get the index's performance. Both managers have to account for the same change, but they don't have to do it through the same trades.

Their fund documents and published holdings let us follow part of that adjustment, including 123,056 Strategy shares reported by three BlackRock funds on Nov. 13, without pretending we know exactly how much stock will be sold at the end of the month.

MSCI's indexes put together stocks that meet a set of rules, such as company size and location, and assign each a share of the index's overall value.

A stock with a larger weight has more influence over how the index performs. The index serves as a benchmark, or performance target, for funds that follow it.

The MSCI USA Index includes large and midsize US companies, and Strategy's Class A shares are scheduled to leave it at the close of trading on Nov. 30, with the change taking effect Dec. 1. MSCI applied new eligibility rules for companies it classifies as non-operating, and Strategy was among the stocks selected for removal.

Other changes to specialized versions of MSCI's indexes are due to be announced on Nov. 18.

BlackRock's iShares MSCI USA ETF (MLRG) follows that US index and trades under the symbol MLRG. As an exchange-traded fund, investors buy and sell shares on a stock exchange while the manager handles the investments inside. Its published holdings included 5,227 Strategy shares on Nov. 13, worth about $583,000.

MLRG uses what's called representative sampling: the manager chooses a collection of investments designed to behave like the index without promising to own every stock on the list at every moment.

Its prospectus, the document setting out how the fund invests, says it intends to keep all or substantially all its assets in index stocks at roughly their index weights. It also allows some investments outside the index when they help the fund follow its performance, including around expected membership changes.

That gives the manager some flexibility while keeping the fund tied to its performance target. Strategy's departure is a reason to adjust the portfolio, but the documents don't require all 5,227 shares reported on Nov. 13 to be sold together at the Nov. 30 close.

BlackRock has another fund that follows the very same index: the iShares MSCI USA Swap UCITS ETF, traded in Europe under symbols including MUSD. This one owns a separate collection of developed-market stocks and uses contracts called total return swaps.

Under its investor document, the fund exchanges that stock portfolio's performance with financial institutions for the performance of the MSCI USA Index.

You're still buying a fund designed to follow MSCI USA, but the contracts provide that connection rather than a portfolio that reproduces the index stock for stock. When Strategy leaves, it stops contributing to the index performance those contracts are meant to deliver.

That doesn't tell us whether MUSD owns Strategy in its separate stock portfolio or whether it will sell any shares.

The counterparties of those contracts may also adjust their own investments to manage the risk they've taken on. Their trades aren't disclosed in these fund documents, so multiplying MUSD's assets by Strategy's index weight wouldn't tell us how many shares the fund has to sell.

BlackRock's iShares MSCI World ETF (URTH) follows companies across developed markets, including the US, and reported 29,345 Strategy shares, worth about $3.3 million, on Nov. 13.

Its iShares MSCI ACWI ETF follows companies in both developed and emerging markets and reported 88,484 shares, worth about $9.9 million, on the same date. These broader indexes include the US segment, so Strategy's removal from MSCI USA also affects them.

Together with MLRG, those funds held 123,056 Strategy shares valued at $13.74 million. We're looking at three identified portfolios on a particular day, rather than every fund affected by MSCI's decision.

Both URTH and ACWI also use representative sampling, so their managers have some flexibility in how they match their indexes.

Reported holdings on Nov. 13, 2026. This is a selected sample of iShares funds, not every MSCI-linked fund or a forecast of shares to be sold.

Source: iShares ACWI holdings, Nov. 13, 2026 · iShares URTH holdings, Nov. 13, 2026 · iShares MLRG holdings, Nov. 13, 2026

The iShares ESG Advanced MSCI USA ETF (USXF) follows a version of MSCI USA that applies additional screening rules to companies. It reported 16,144 Strategy shares on Nov. 13, but as of Nov. 17, the standard-index announcement doesn't establish what will happen in this particular version.

Thanks for signing up to The Catalyst. Look out for your first daily email. If you already receive it, you’re all set.

MSCI's announcement for those specialized indexes is still due Nov. 18, so USXF isn't included in the three-fund subtotal.

Investors holding Strategy through a fund tied to another index don't automatically face the same change. For example, Invesco QQQ follows the Nasdaq-100, which has its own provider and membership rules.

Managers paid to choose stocks themselves can also keep assessing Strategy on their own terms, as can anyone who owns its shares directly.

Approximate Strategy holdings per $10,000 of fund assets on Nov. 13, 2026: reported portfolio weight divided by 100, then multiplied by $10,000. Inputs are rounded by iShares. These amounts are not forecasts of losses or required sales. USXF follows a screened index; its specific deletion treatment remains pending the Nov. 18 announcement as of Nov. 17.

Source: iShares USXF holdings, Nov. 13, 2026 · iShares MLRG holdings, Nov. 13, 2026 · iShares URTH holdings, Nov. 13, 2026 · iShares ACWI holdings, Nov. 13, 2026

In its response to MSCI's consultation, Strategy said that funds following the provider's global investable indexes held about 13 million of its shares, equivalent to 3.1% of basic shares outstanding.

That's a much broader estimate than the three-fund sample here, but the published statement doesn't identify the individual funds or give a current observation date for their holdings.

After the index changes, daily holdings files will let us compare what these funds owned before and afterward. Those files can show that a portfolio has fewer Strategy shares, but they won't necessarily show how the shares left it or why.

ETFs can grow or shrink as investors put money in or take it out. When a fund grows, its Strategy holding could increase simply because it needs more of the stocks it already owns.

Comparing the number of Strategy shares with the number of the fund's own shares helps separate fund growth from changes in how much of its portfolio it assigns to Strategy.

When an ETF shrinks, some stocks can leave through the process used to redeem its shares. Financial institutions can hand fund shares back to the ETF and receive underlying securities in return.

Strategy stock could leave the ETF without the fund itself selling it on an exchange, and the institution receiving that stock would then decide what to do with it. The next holdings file would record the smaller position without telling us about those later decisions.

MUSD adds another limit to what we can observe because its contracts deliver the index performance. Its counterparties could adjust their investments as Strategy leaves, but following only the fund's stock holdings wouldn't capture those decisions.

Even when we can see holdings change, comparing two dates won't show how much of Strategy's share-price movement was driven by MSCI, especially when investors can trade ahead of the announced change.

Strategy will still lose a place in the performance target these funds are paid to follow.

That could weaken demand for its stock and make raising money less attractive for a company that sells securities to finance Bitcoin purchases, although the index removal doesn't require Strategy to sell any Bitcoin itself.

#5018. German lawmakers back crypto freezes outside criminal cases

Customs authorities could hold “suspicious” assets for 30 days under the bill, with court oversight for extensions and disputed confiscation.

Germany’s lower house of parliament has passed a bill that would let customs authorities temporarily freeze cryptocurrency and other high-value assets suspected of having unlawful origins without first opening a criminal investigation.

The Bundestag passed the customs reform bill on Friday as part of a wider effort to combat money laundering and organized crime. The proposed procedure would target assets worth more than 100,000 euros and explicitly mentions cryptocurrencies.

Under the bill’s text approved by lawmakers, authorities would be able to hold assets for up to 30 days where there are factual indications of unlawful origins, according to a translated version. However, filing an application for confiscation could suspend those deadlines pending a court decision, and in contested cases, a court would have to be satisfied that the assets were of unlawful origin before ordering confiscation, effectively putting the burden of proof on the crypto holder.

German Social Democratic Party lawmaker Ingo Vogel said that the powers would allow authorities to pursue suspicious assets even when there are not yet grounds to open a criminal case, according to the Bundestag’s summary of the debate on the bill.

The bill still requires consent from the Bundesrat, Germany’s upper house of parliament, and is intended to take effect on Jan. 1, 2027.

Germany’s Federal Bar Association, known as BRAK, previously opposed the government’s draft in an Oct. 28 statement, warning that the meaning of unlawful origin is too vague and risks treating missing records as evidence of illicit wealth.

The association pointed to assets inherited through generations as one example where owners may lack a paper trail. It also questioned what the administrative process would add to Germany’s existing criminal confiscation rules.

German blockchain industry association Bundesblock also raised concerns about the treatment of digital assets in a March 31 submission on an earlier draft. It warned at the time that blockchain analysis should not automatically be treated as proof of ownership or control, and that incorrect wallet attribution could even infringe fundamental rights.

Related: Crypto adoption blooming in Germany, while UK is falling ‘behind,’ says CoinShares researcher

Germany has already carried out large crypto seizures under existing law. As Cointelegraph reported, Saxony authorities sold 49,858 Bitcoin (BTC) linked to the Movie2k piracy investigation in 2024, raising about 2.6 billion euros, or $2.8 billion. At the time, prosecutors said the proceeds remained secured pending a court ruling on confiscation.

In a recent development, local outlet MDR reported on Friday that a Leipzig judge proposed ending proceedings against the main defendant in exchange for 40,000 BTC and a payment of 38 million euros for the potential victims. The proposal remains under consideration.

#5017. 'Tokenization Is Not the Finish Line': Jupiter to Let Users Borrow Against Bullish Shares

'Tokenization Is Not the Finish Line': Jupiter to Let Users Borrow Against Bullish Shares

Jupiter, the largest trading platform on Solana, is bringing Bullish's shares onchain as collateral, as part of a push to put tokenized assets to work.

The company will launch a dedicated, permissioned market on its lending platform, Jupiter Lend, starting with Bullish's NYSE-listed BLSH stock, Jupiter tweeted on Monday. More issuer tokens will follow, though the market won't be available in all jurisdictions, it added.

A NYSE-listed company is bringing its own shares directly to Jupiter Lend.

Today at Breakpoint, we announced our partnership with @Bullish to launch a dedicated, permissioned $BLSH market.

For the first time, Issuer Tokens can be used as collateral inside Solana’s… pic.twitter.com/rWWqwOcWmK

— Jupiter (@JupiterExchange) November 16, 2026

Unlike many tokenized stocks, which give holders a claim on a share, Bullish's issuer-sponsored token "is itself the share," Jupiter COO Kash Dhanda said in a presentation at Solana's Breakpoint conference in London.

Users will be able to borrow against them with fully onchain liquidations in an "institutional-grade lending market," and integrations with qualified custodians, he said. Bullish acquired Equiniti, one of the world's largest transfer agents, earlier this year, Dhanda noted.

Dhanda framed the announcements around what he called the "post-tokenization era." Most tokenized assets today are "parked, not productive," he said.

Of the roughly $460 billion in tokenized assets tracked by data platform RWA.xyz, only about $39.5 billion is actually onchain and can be moved off the issuer's platform, and just $3.4 billion is used in DeFi, according to DeFiLlama, Dhanda said, a "utilization gap" of 99%.

"There is this myth, and this is the thing that's misunderstood: 'If you put it on chain, they will come'," he said. "This is not the field of dreams," he added, arguing that, "Tokenization is not the finish line. It is actually the starting line."

Jupiter launched two other products alongside the Bullish market. The Jupiter Global Passport lets users verify their identity to buy permissioned assets, while keeping their information as private as possible using zero-knowledge data sharing, Dhanda said. It is live with KYC verification, with onchain credit scores and proof of wealth to follow, and the company is exploring licenses in different jurisdictions.

Jupiter Liquidity Services, meanwhile, will help asset issuers design their markets, seed initial capital, find market makers and integrate with Jupiter's routing so that their tokens are available across the platforms that use it. "You integrate once, you will be available everywhere," Dhanda said.

"Shallow credit markets don't drive liquidity on chain," he added. "If you cannot do more with your onchain asset than you can do with the off-chain version of it, you're probably not going to switch."

Jupiter says it has handled more than $500 billion in trading volume so far this year and paid out $162 million in yield. The Breakpoint announcements follow the company's launch last week of token baskets, yield vaults and a rebuilt portfolio, and come as other venues bring tokenized stocks to Solana. Trading platform Formation has notified the SEC of plans to trade tokenized U.S. stocks on the network.

Jupiter powers token swaps on The Information Exchange, Decrypt's trading platform.

#5015. Three wallets hoard $52.7M on XRP’s sidechain, and nobody is trading it

Three addresses control nearly $53 million in USDf on XRPL EVM, raising questions about liquidity concentration and XRP demand.

Three addresses hold virtually all the dollar-pegged USDf token supply on XRP Ledger (XRPL) EVM, an XRP-powered smart contract sidechain, according to a Nov. 17 explorer snapshot.

The contract contains 52.9 million tokens, while DefiLlama values the chain's tracked bridged stablecoin inventory at about $52.7 million.

DefiLlama reports $22,415 in total value locked (TLV) in tracked DeFi protocols and just $0.09 in chain fees over 24 hours. Tokens are present, but measured application activity and fee expenditure remain small.

XRPL EVM is a separate blockchain from the native XRP Ledger. Its official documentation describes a sovereign layer-1 that runs Ethereum-compatible smart contracts and uses XRP for transaction fees.

That gives XRP a direct role in operating the chain, without making every dollar bridged there a dollar spent buying XRP.

On Nov. 17, the USDf contract metadata showed a supply of 52,906,708 tokens. The holder list showed four balances: 40 million USDf in the largest, about 7 million in the second, and 5.9 million in the third.

Those positions represent about 75.6%, 13.25%, and 11.15% of supply, respectively. The fourth address, labeled SquidMulticall, held one smallest unit, or 0.000000000000000001 USDf.

Anthropic’s IPO unlocks test Arthur Hayes’s $1.245 trillion AI selling scenario and its potential impact on Bitcoin liquidity.

Anthropic’s planned IPO brings a real risk of insider selling, but its share-release schedule does not make a drain on Bitcoin liquidity inevitable.

Arthur Hayes’s Nov. 5 essay puts falling AI share prices at the start of a broader credit squeeze. He argues that insider sales will weaken stocks, make borrowing more expensive or unavailable, curb bank-balance-sheet growth, and reduce the dollar liquidity supporting crypto.

Hayes estimated 83% dilution by June 2027, arguing that roughly $1.245 trillion in new capital would be needed to absorb potential selling at a hypothetical $1.5 trillion IPO valuation.

Anthropic provides a concrete test of the first link, since its offering creates new shares, while subsequent releases also permit existing holders to sell.

Those changes affect supply differently, with different consequences for company fundraising and investors’ ownership.

Anthropic’s Nov. 10 announcement proposes 825 million Class A shares, with 801,351,354 offered by the company and 23,648,646 by existing stockholders, and the AI firm receives no proceeds from the existing holders’ sales.

The preliminary price range is $70 to $78, with an option for underwriters to purchase another 123.75 million shares.

New company shares increase the outstanding share count and raise money for Anthropic. Secondary shares already exist, and selling them transfers ownership and pays the selling holder. A later unlock removes a restriction on selling without issuing another share.

Anthropic proposes new company shares alongside existing-holder shares. Follow each transaction to see who receives the proceeds.

801,351,354 shares offered by Anthropic: the company receives the purchase proceeds and issues new stock.

23,648,646 shares offered by existing stockholders: the selling holders receive the proceeds; Anthropic receives none.

New issuance raises company capital; a secondary sale pays the selling holder. Resale eligibility alone is not a cash-flow measure.

#5011. Custodia Bank loses Supreme Court bid for direct Fed payment access

The Supreme Court refused to hear Custodia Bank’s appeal, meaning a lower court ruling allowing the Fed to reject account applications will stand.

The United States Supreme Court on Monday declined to hear an appeal from crypto-focused bank Custodia, effectively ending the bank’s latest legal effort to gain direct access to the Federal Reserve’s payment system.

Custodia is a Wyoming-chartered bank founded by Caitlin Long. The bank has been trying for a Fed master account since 2020, which would allow it to process payments directly without relying on third-party financial institutions.

Now, the Supreme Court’s Monday decision means an earlier ruling allowing the Fed to reject applications from eligible banks will remain in effect.

The case highlights some of the challenges crypto-facing banks face in gaining direct access to the US payment system. Still, even if state-chartered banks qualify for master accounts, the Fed does not have to approve every application.

In a dissent issued in March, US Circuit Judge Timothy Tymkovich criticized the appeals court’s decision to give Federal Reserve banks discretion over master accounts.

“Without a master account, a bank cannot operate in the modern banking system,” Tymkovich wrote, arguing that the ruling effectively gives the Fed the power to override state banking decisions.

Custodia first sued the Federal Reserve in 2022 after waiting around two years for a decision on its master account application. The Federal Reserve Bank of Kansas City ended up rejecting the request in January 2023, citing concerns about risks linked to the bank’s crypto-focused business model.

In October 2025, a federal appeals court ruled against Custodia, finding that Federal Reserve banks did not have to grant master accounts to every eligible institution.

Related: Crypto among sectors ‘debanked’ by 9 major banks: US regulator

Cointelegraph previously reported that the court declined to reconsider its decision in March. This led Custodia to take its case to the Supreme Court.

The bank’s appeal also received support from the Blockchain Association, which argued that the Fed’s ability to reject applications could weaken the authority of state banking regulators.

Senator Cynthia Lummis and former Senator Patrick Toomey also filed a brief with the Supreme Court in August, supporting Custodia’s appeal.

Today’s decision comes as other crypto-focused banks seek access to the Fed’s payment system. In March, Kraken Financial received approval for a restricted account from the Federal Reserve Bank of Kansas City — the same regional bank that rejected Custodia’s application.

Notably, Kraken’s account was approved for an initial one-year period and allows it to send and receive payments through the Fed’s Fedwire system. However, the account has restrictions and does not offer all the services of a full master account.

Looking ahead, Custodia may still be able to apply for another master account or seek limited access to the Fed’s payment system under a separate proposal.

#5010. Saylor’s Strategy Keeps Buying Bitcoin, Adding 'A Little Orange' Through the Dip

Saylor’s Strategy Keeps Buying Bitcoin, Adding 'A Little Orange' Through the Dip

Strategy kept buying Bitcoin through a brutal market stretch, adding 485 BTC worth roughly $33.4 million and repurchasing $228 million of its preferred stock, as chairman Michael Saylor urged the market to rally with a characteristically cheeky nudge.

The company disclosed the purchase in a filing Monday. The modest addition, small by the standards of a firm that once bought tens of thousands of coins at a time, lifted Strategy’s total holdings to 850,849 BTC as of Nov. 15, alongside $4.9 billion in U.S. dollar assets.

Strategy, the largest corporate holder of Bitcoin, remains far ahead of any other treasury company.

The buy caps a stretch of smaller, steadier accumulation paired with stock buybacks. Strategy recently added $82 million in Bitcoin while repurchasing $188 million of its STRC preferred shares, part of a shift toward what it calls a capital-management approach, buying back stock when it views the shares as undervalued rather than relentlessly stacking coins.

Bitcoin has slid sharply in recent days, trading well below the six-figure highs it touched earlier in the cycle, and the downturn has squeezed Bitcoin treasury firms whose valuations rise and fall with the asset.

Saylor, undeterred, posted the holdings update to X alongside the firm’s trademark Bitcoin tracker, and followed it with a quip aimed at the slumping market: “This dip could use a little orange,” a nod to Bitcoin’s signature color.

The purchase lands during a precarious moment for the treasury-company model Strategy pioneered. Index provider MSCI has finalized rules that could eject Bitcoin treasury firms like Strategy from its widely tracked equity indexes, classifying companies whose balance sheets are dominated by a single asset as “non-operating” and therefore ineligible.

Removal would force index-tracking funds to sell the affected shares, potentially pressuring prices and shrinking the premium these firms have long commanded over the value of their Bitcoin.

For now, Strategy is doing what it has always done, buying Bitcoin and talking it up, even as the market tests its conviction.

The combination of a small purchase and a sizable buyback underscores the balancing act: keep accumulating, defend the stock, and weather a downturn that has turned the once-unstoppable treasury trade into a far more fraught proposition.
