#4887. Want Studio-Style Pilates at Home? Start With These Editor-Tested Reformers

Our top picks for every kind of at-home Pilates setup, from compact machines to studio-worthy reformers.

Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

If you’re a pilates princess, you already know what a reformer is, and you’re well acquainted with the many ways it delivers a low-impact, strength-building workout. However, if you’re a newbie, here’s a quick crash course: A reformer is a specially designed machine, originally developed by Joseph Pilates, that consists of springs for resistance, a moving carriage, a foot bar that you push or pull, and pulleys to hold onto or hook to your feet when performing pilates exercises.

“I’d describe the reformer as a machine designed to help create an understanding of your body with resistance,” says Sam Miles, owner and co-founder of Good Time Pilates in New York City. “It gives real time feedback so you can find sensation through the shortening and lengthening of your muscles. In short and easy terms: an assist to finding your muscle engagement!”

There are unique benefits to using a reformer that are hard to replicate in a pilates mat workout, or really any other type of workout. But that doesn’t mean you have to be advanced to start using one. “The modifications to increase or decrease challenge make it a truly universal machine for any body and any fitness level, which is very unique and just awesome,” Miles says. “You can rehabilitate with a reformer, strengthen muscles, stretch and find release work, it’s the best!”

Pilates reformers are available in different types: classical and contemporary. The classical reformer stays true to Joseph Pilates’ original design; the machines are made of wood, and have springs that all have the exact same resistance level. Purists are going to want to consider these machines.

Contemporary reformers are an evolutionary riff on the original and often incorporate springs of varying resistance that can be adjusted. The dimensions also usually vary a bit from the OG classical reformer design.

While it used to be that reformers were only found in Pilates studios, more and more women are investing in a reformer as an addition to their home gym setup. There are also less intense reformer models on the market that are specifically designed for at-home use, and these generally come in at a fraction of the cost of a classical or studio-grade contemporary reformer.

After testing a bunch of options, we narrowed down our picks to a variety of machines, including commercial-grade reformers and pared-down, reimagined reformers that are made specifically to take up less space and be more affordable.

After testing a handful of Pilates reformers, the contemporary-style Balanced Body Allegro 2 came out on top for its studio-quality, strong springs, durable build, and versatile foot bar. WH fitness contributor Talene Appleton has been using it two to three times a week to practice at home for almost two years, and it’s still in mint condition. Appleton says it’s built like a tank and is commercial-grade, so it’s the best you can get for your at-home gym setup.

Five springs are featured for varying tension to accommodate different levels—three high resistance (red), one medium resistance (blue), and one light resistance (yellow), while the steel, grippy foot bar glides effortlessly for 10 vertical and horizontal positions. “I was blown away by how much the additional positions of its foot bar allowed me to change up my usual Pilates sequences,” says Appleton. “This adds incredible versatility in terms of movement options that most competitors can’t beat.” While the foot bar is its best feature, Appleton notes it’s the most difficult to set up and requires two people to line it up evenly on each side.Appleton says this machine is best for advanced users, given there’s a bit of a learning curve at first. “Using a traditional reformer at home can be a bit overwhelming at first, especially if you’re used to having an instructor call the shots in terms of spring resistance, foot bar positions, moves, and all the rest,” she says. “I found myself second-guessing my setup and wondering if I was getting the most out of each exercise (or sometimes if the move I was doing was even a real exercise at all).” She credits YouTube and TikTok tutorials for guiding her along, specifically from Balanced Body and East River Pilates.While this is the best Pilates machine money can buy (with a steep price tag of $4,345 *sigh*) it’s heavy at 157 pounds. It’s also large, at eight feet long and three feet wide, so make sure you have adequate space before splurging. It’s also not the easiest to set up. “Setting this thing up was no joke—I knew I was in for a challenge when I saw the multiple massive, heavy boxes it arrived in,” Appleton says. She notes it took her and a friend two hours to assemble.

Read More: Balanced Body Allegro 2 Review

The classical Merrithew At Home SPX Reformer is next-level if you want to up your Pilates game. It features a foldable vertical tower, which can improve flexibility and target different muscle groups with more controlled movements, adding more challenge. It has five springs—four full-resistance and one with half-resistance. Given the springs mostly have the same resistance, this machine is designed for more advanced users.

The foot bar is adjustable with four positions for different heights, while the carriage is padded for comfort. Another call-out is the included reformer box, which adds height and range of motion to moves in the seated and lying position. It’s especially helpful for those with muscle tightness or who need to modify moves involving the knees.

While this is a great reformer to elevate your practice, it’s quite large at 96 inches long and 26 inches wide. It’s also heavy at 115 pounds. Like the AeroPilates Pro XP 557, this isn’t ideal for apartments. The tower structure also requires more vertical space, so if you don’t have high ceilings, our best overall is most likely your best bet.

Read More: Best Compact Home Gym Equipment

Pretty much all pilates reformers in this guide are relatively large, but the contemporary AeroPilates Reformer 4420 is foldable. If you’re an apartment dweller, this machine is your compact answer to your Pilates reformer dreams. It can be stashed under a couch, bed, or behind a door. At 69 pounds, it’s not the lightest, so having two people for setup is probably your best bet.

Like the AeroPilates Reformer 287, it uses cords, not springs, yet delivers impressive effectiveness. This model has four adjustable cords with varying resistances and color codes, unlike the 287: two standard resistances (black), one extra intensity (red), and one light resistance (yellow). So, this reformer is good for both beginners and those who are more advanced.

It also has a built-in cardio rebounder, which is essentially a mini trampoline at the foot bar, making it an especially good choice for someone looking for low-impact cardio options and variety.

The contemporary Your Reformer is studio-grade like our best overall reformer pick, and is super durable despite being a little over half the price. During a stay in Los Angeles, Appleton rented one for at-home workouts and was extremely impressed with its easily changeable five thick springs, and a carriage that glides smoothly and quietly. The springs are also color-coded: two heavy resistance (red), two medium resistance (blue), and one light resistance (yellow).

In terms of quality, it’s a direct competitor to the Allegro 2. “The straps are thick and definitely won’t fray on me, and the strap handles are comfortable to grip, even when my palms get sweaty,” Appleton says. It’s not compact enough for most apartments, but it’s slimmer to accommodate home spaces better.

Appleton is 5’5” and found the carriage to be wide and spacious, with plenty of room to move around from supine to standing to kneeling positions. It also accommodates her much taller boyfriend, who’s “20 times more passionate about a good reformer workout,” so it’s the real deal.

The AeroPilates Reformer 287 is the most affordable option we’ve come across. It’s dramatically less expensive than our best overall—it costs under $400! But that doesn’t mean it’s less effective. Its quality is still impressive, just not studio-grade. WH entertainment editor Amy Wilkinson, an avid Pilates practitioner, was surprised by how sturdy this machine is because of its bargain price, and since it comes pre-assembled (another plus).

But, she stresses it’s best for beginners since it only features three resistance cords. “I could see someone eventually progressing beyond the capabilities of this model, especially when it comes to exercises like footwork and running, which are classically done on four springs,” says Wilkinson. “It also lacks certain accessories you’d typically find with a studio machine—a box, which is typically used for exercises in the short-box series and in a long position for pulling straps and T-press, among others.”

Speaking of resistance, unlike our best overall, this reformer uses cords instead of springs. While they can be trickier to hook on and off, their weight is identical to springs Wilkinson uses on studio-grade models.The carriage glides smoothly, although Wilkinson notes the attached handles would fall and get in the way. She recommends tossing them aside instead of hanging on the built-in shoulder blocks. As for the foot bar, it’s stable but can’t be adjusted for specific exercises.Aside from mechanics, this reformer is extremely compact, weighing just 56 pounds, and measuring 42 inches when folded and 85 inches fully extended. Wilkinson lives in a one-bedroom Brooklyn apartment and has no issues stashing it away, although she finds it tricky to fold and wide when the foot bar is attached.AeroPilates says this product can fit people up to 6'4", but Wilkinson, who is 5’11”, says even her height was pushing the machine’s limits. “I imagine anyone much taller than I am would feel a bit crunched,” she says. She also says it’s narrow, and didn’t have additional breathing room.

While most full-sized pilates reformers don’t have a built-in trampoline at the foot bar, the contemporary AeroPilates Pro XP 557 is the first full-sized model we’ve seen with a rebounder, so cardio moves like single-leg pushups and slow squats can be added to the routine. This is especially useful for beginners getting into the groove. WH associate visual editor Berkeley Brooks found it stayed sturdy when executing explosive movements at fast paces, while the material of the main carriage prevented her from slipping around.

Brooks notes that the four strong springs are easily interchangeable and have varying resistances labeled by color: two low resistance (blue) and two high resistance (yellow). The foot bar is adjustable, thick, and quiet for added comfort, and can be placed in three positions to accommodate different heights without disrupting your range of motion.

The platform is also wide at 23 inches and long at 100 inches, so this model isn’t ideal for small apartments, especially since you need additional space to execute exercises.

On the upside, Brooks says it’s easy to build and aesthetically pleasing. “I love the addition of wood to the machine because it looks great in a home gym,” she adds.

The springs in a pilates reformer are an important consideration when you’re choosing your machine. “Springs provide resistance and feedback, so the type and responsiveness of springs deeply influence your experience,” says Mo Wolfe, owner and Pilates instructor of Evolution Pilates in Port Washington, New York.

The weight of springs can also depend on whether a machine is classical or contemporary. Classical style reformers have a heavier spring tension that is the same throughout, while modern models generally tend to offer springs with a variety of resistance levels. A reformer with springs is the type you’ll find in a Pilates studio.

Alternatively, resistance cords are sometimes used in the place of springs in reformer machines that are designed for personal and at-home use. They offer similar effectiveness and are more affordable.

Taking the size of your home into consideration is important before purchasing a Pilates machine. Not only do you want to make sure you have enough room for the machine itself, you also want to make sure there will be enough space to perform the full range of Pilates reformer exercises, like leg circles, that require room to move.

Some reformers are very big and bulky, such as our pro-level, best overall selection. They take up considerable real estate and they’re best for a home gym where they can become a more permanent fixture that won’t need to be moved once it’s installed.

If your workout space is multi-functional (i.e., it’s your living room) and your equipment needs to have a smaller footprint and be more portable so you can move it around or stash it away, look for a lighter, foldable option. Just make sure that you’ll have enough space to do the moves when it’s all set up.

Since reformer Pilates is a low-impact activity, and the resistance can be so fine-tuned for your fitness level, there are no hard and fast rules about how often you do a reformer session each week. Miles says it really comes down to how your body feels. “With the variety you can get from a reformer, daily use is manageable. At my studio we have challenging classes, stretch and release classes, technique-focused classes; variety is important!” She notes that most of her clients do three reformer sessions per week.

We picked the brains of Pilates instructors to understand what to look for when shopping for a reformer, then researched dozens of the top-rated models. From there, Women’s Health writers and editors (including fitness contributors Nicolette Accardi and Talene Appleton, and entertainment editor Amy Wilkinson) tested some of the best themselves to narrow down the options.

During testing, they paid close attention to spring and cord resistance level as a measure of whether or not the machines were ideal for beginners or more advanced users. The testers also considered size, durability, and ease of assembly to determine what sorts of spaces were needed for these machiness. Moves like planks, triceps presses, running (pushing off the foot bar), chest expansions, and leg circles were all completed during our testing Pilates workouts to really put these machine to the test.

#4884. Bitcoin drops 2.5% as Nvidia stock risks new 5-month lows into Q3 earnings

Bitcoin price downside sees local lows of $63,269 as Nvidia stock targets $150 as traders brace for volatility over Q3 earnings.

Bitcoin saw selling pressure after Tuesday’s Wall Street open as stock markets stayed on edge ahead of Nvidia’s third-quarter earnings and forward guidance.

Data from TradingView showed BTC/USD dipping to $63,269 on Bitstamp, down up to 2.5% on the day.

BTC/USD one-hour chart. Source: Cointelegraph/TradingView

US equities saw minor losses as the session began, with traders eyeing key data from Nvidia, along with cues as to how the company planned to handle the ongoing controversy surrounding its former CEO Jensen Huang.

Amid mounting pressure to reinstate Huang despite resistance from US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, commentators saw little chance of Nvidia’s board reversing its decision to dismiss him.

On Tuesday, the board announced the creation of a National Security and Export Control Oversight Committee, dedicated to “oversight of the company’s national security policies, export control compliance and global trade risk management.”

“We are committed to working constructively with government and industry partners to help establish and advance a robust framework that uses every tool at our disposal to safeguard national security while supporting continued technological innovation,” board chairman Harvey Jones commented in a press release.

Huang will also appear to testify before Congress on Dec. 1. In its latest analysis, trading resource The Kobeissi Letter put the odds of Huang returning at less than 20% in light of the latest events.

“Any indication that the probability is higher would be strongly bullish for the stock,” it wrote on X.

Kobeissi queried whether Huang’s departure could justify the $750 billion loss in market cap Nvidia had suffered, with NVDA dipping to $150.35, down over 3% on the day. On Nov. 12, it hit $148.80, its lowest since late June.

Nvidia stock one-hour chart. Source: Cointelegraph/TradingView

Market nerves extended beyond the US ahead of a key moment for the AI sector. South Korea’s tech-heavy KOSPI Composite Index finished Tuesday’s trading session 2.6% lower at 4,968 points — its lowest daily close since Feb. 2.

KOSPI one-day chart. Source: Cointelegraph/TradingView

“The tape feels increasingly fragile as Nvidia’s AI premium continues to unwind and investors reassess the durability of the ecosystem built around its dominance,” CNBC quoted FedWatch Advisors founder Ben Emons as stating in a note.

CNBC and others referenced data from Bank of America’s latest monthly fund manager survey, which showed that investors slashed tech-stock exposure last month from 37% to 12% overweight tech — the largest single monthly reduction since June 2006.

BTC price action sought to break down from its narrow range between $64,000 and $66,000, in place since Nov. 15, as traders awaited Nvidia signals.

Related: Bitcoin realized loss metric beats June high as open interest eyes 2-year low

In an X update on the day, Keith Alan, cofounder of crypto trading platform Material Indicators, stipulated that the market needed to fulfil several key conditions as part of a durable rebound.

BTC/USD, he argued, should reclaim its 200-week simple moving average (SMA) at $67,977, but that this alone was not “enough.” Lower time frames must also produce a series of higher swing lows and higher swing highs, with breakouts through local resistance accompanied by high buyer volume.

“Until then, a bounce has a higher probability of being a trap than a legit recovery effort,” Alan summarized.

There are a lot of laser hair removal devices on the market, which is why you should consider a few of these pointers before investing.

IPL and diode lasers both slow hair growth and reduce the thickness of individual strands by scanning for pigment and targeting the hair follicle, says dermatologist Melanie Kingsley, MD. But, they each have their benefits and limitations.

IPL is the most commonly used type of light in at-home laser hair removal devices. This technology uses broad-spectrum light to target melanin, the pigment that gives your hair its color. The light is also unsuitable for dark and deep skin tones because it can’t distinguish between melanin-rich skin and the pigment of dark hair, says dermatologist Rachel Nazarian, MD. However, if you have a fair to olive complexion with dark hair, then you’re an ideal candidate for IPL treatments.

Until recently, all at-home laser hair removal devices were IPL lasers. But Epilaser has a game-changing laser for home use. Unlike IPL lights, which emit a broad spectrum of light ranging from 400 to 1,400 nm, diode lasers are unique because they use a more concentrated wavelength of light (around 810 nm). This precise wavelength means it can better target the hair follicles rather than accidentally burning your skin, making it more accessible for some people with darker complexions.

Both are effective, but diode lasers are slightly more versatile. That said, no matter which one you go with, you’ll need multiple treatments to maintain your hair-free results.

One of the biggest considerations is the number of flashes a device is equipped to deliver. This number indicates how long the device will last, according to Dr. Nazarian. One of the best ways to reduce discomfort during laser hair removal is to use cooling technology. It lowers your skin’s temperature—before, during, and after each laser pulse—to help you better tolerate longer and higher treatment settings safely.

Devices with bigger heads are more efficient on large areas. If you have sensitive skin, consider stretching your treatments out to once a month to start and gradually up the frequency once your skin can handle the laser hair removal treatment. The final hair-free results will take longer to achieve but at least you won’t risk irritating your skin. FWIW, she says you’ll notice thinning hair after your first four treatments.

Once you choose your device, know that it can take some time to see results. While every device is different, you’ll probably use it weekly anywhere from four to 10 weeks before noticing lasting results, says dermatologist Bertha Baum, DO. The final results might take longer to achieve, but you won’t risk irritating your skin. This technology has come a long way and, while pricey, it's a long-term investment that pays for itself. Think of it this way: A laser that costs $500 is basically the same price as a professional hair removal session, and that in-office treatment won't last forever, but you will continue using your at-home laser for years. After testing these devices since February 2022, beauty director Brian Underwood, deputy deals and trends editor Eunice Lucero-Lee, and luxury commerce editor Sarah Maberry whittled down this list to 12 of the best laser hair removal devices. We also tapped contributors Jasmine Gomez, Lily Wohlner, and Brigitt Earley to ensure these devices work across most skin tones.

They all boast impressive features, are comfortable to use, and offer incredible value. Plus, these picks are FDA-cleared, so they’ve been evaluated for safety and efficacy. Several dermatologists also shared their no-fail laser hair removal tips and best-in-class product recommendations.

And because we know what it’s like to ball on a budget, we also considered pricing. TBH, laser hair removal devices aren’t exactly cheap. Many cost between $300 and $600, especially when shopping for these expert-approved devices from well-respected brands, such as Braun.

To help, I carefully researched dozens of other cheaper, yet top-rated Amazon laser hair removal devices. For added peace of mind, they all earned thousands of rave reviews from real Amazon customers.

So if you're ready to ditch daily shaving and bi-monthly waxing, we're confident—based on our own testing and our dermatologists' advice—that this list contains only the best, most effective options on the market worth your hard-earned coins.

Dr. Nazarian confirms at-home laser hair removal devices are generally safe and effective, citing a 2019 paper. The biggest challenge with many at-home devices comes down to their inability to differentiate between dark skin and dark hair due to their pigmentation. Melanin-rich complexions risk absorbing too much laser energy that increases the risk for burning, cautions Dr. Nazarian. If this is you, then see your dermatologist for a recommendation on the best laser hair removal treatments and devices.

It's also a good idea to do a patch test and not expose the treated area to sunlight for a week, says Dr. Shirazi. Your treated skin is temporarily more sensitive, and you risk sunburn, hyperpigmentation, and delayed healing. She also doesn’t suggest using the laser on tanned and tattooed skin, open wounds, moles, or birthmarks to avoid changing their appearance or causing accidental burns.

#4882. Jensen Huang Says He'd Be 'Honored' to Return as Nvidia CEO, Despite Board's Resistance

Jensen Huang Says He'd Be 'Honored' to Return as Nvidia CEO, Despite Board's Resistance

Jensen Huang said Tuesday he would be willing to return as Nvidia CEO, publicly addressing the campaign to reinstate him less than a week after his abrupt departure. His offer came despite reports that the chipmaker's board has no plans to bring him back.

“If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO,” Huang wrote in a statement on X.

The Nvidia co-founder also apologized for the conduct that triggered his exit. “I did not live up to the standards expected of everyone at NVIDIA, and I have made serious mistakes in my personal life,” he wrote. “I created problems for the Board that I deeply regret.”

“I own my mistakes completely, and I am committed to cooperating with the Board’s independent investigation,” he added.

Over the past week, I’ve been overwhelmed by the love and support of friends, industry colleagues, and people I've never met. Thank you to everyone who has shown kindness to my family and me. It means the world to me.

I came to the United States 53 years ago, and becoming an…

— Jensen Huang (@JensenHuang) November 17, 2026

His X profile underwent a separate change around the same time. By Tuesday, Huang had removed “CEO” from his bio, which now identifies him only as “Founder of NVIDIA”; the company banner and corporate affiliation badge also disappeared.

Huang resigned last Thursday after 33 years leading the chipmaker he founded in 1993. His departure followed disclosures about extramarital relationships involving Nvidia employees and a business executive whom U.S. officials suspect of connections to Chinese intelligence. Those intelligence allegations have not been established as fact.

The board's independent investigation is examining his conduct and whether sensitive company information or national security were put at risk. Nvidia has said it has no reason to believe company secrets were compromised; chief financial officer Colette Kress is serving as interim CEO.

“Since my departure, I’ve seen an outpouring of calls from NVIDIA’s employees, investors, business partners, and customers for me to return as CEO,” Huang wrote. He said many were reaching out directly as Nvidia navigates “complex technology, market, competitive, and geopolitical dynamics.” “NVIDIA is a once-in-a-generation company,” he added.

But the board's position—at least as of Tuesday—is that directors are focused on the investigation, not reinstatement.

The company is simultaneously looking for a successor. Directors reportedly approached Arm CEO Rene Haas, a former Nvidia executive, according to the Financial Times, although Nvidia said it had not formally engaged candidates and called speculation premature.

The movement to restore Huang has nevertheless attracted powerful allies. President Donald Trump said Monday he “would certainly not mind” a comeback, while Elon Musk backed a petition demanding Huang's reinstatement that had drawn nearly 192,000 signatures by Monday.

OpenAI CEO Sam Altman offered a more qualified defense. Altman, who was briefly fired and reinstated at OpenAI in 2023, said Huang had “long been a hero of mine” and that “heroes have flaws,” but stopped short of saying Nvidia should rehire him.

Huang also made a patriotic appeal, especially considering his outsting was especially rushed not because of his affairs but because of the possibility of him leaking secrets to China. “I came to the United States 53 years ago, and becoming an American citizen is one of the greatest gifts and proudest moments of my life,” he wrote.

“NVIDIA has been my life’s work,” he continued. “Nowhere but in America could a company like NVIDIA be possible. I love our country, and I love NVIDIA.”

He closed by thanking supporters and telling his family, “I love you, and I will spend the rest of my life being worthy of yours.” Nvidia, meanwhile, is continuing its permanent CEO search, with Kress scheduled to lead the company's quarterly earnings call later today.

#4879. Moderate To Severe Hot Flashes Due To Menopause Are Worth Treating. Work With Your Doctor To Develop A Plan

A Bayer-paid spokesperson, OB-GYN, and menopause specialist explains why hot flashes due to menopause happen, how long they can last, and how to prepare for discussions about treatment options with your doctor.

Branded content for Lynkuet® (elinzanetant) 60 mg capsules. Keep reading for Important Safety Information.

For women, menopause is a natural stage of life and is diagnosed when a woman hasn’t had a period for 12 months and can no longer get pregnant. Menopause is not a disease or disorder—it’s a natural part of aging. It’s estimated that over 2 million women in the U.S. enter menopause each year. Almost 50 percent of women in their first year of menopause experience moderate to severe hot flashes.

Diana Bitner, MD, OB-GYN, is a Bayer-paid spokesperson and has been compensated for her time.

But, moderate to severe hot flashes don’t have to be something you simply endure, says Diana Bitner, MD, OB-GYN, a menopause specialist and Bayer-paid spokesperson. There are treatment options available, such as Lynkuet® (elinzanetant), an FDA-approved, hormone-free prescription treatment for the reduction of moderate to severe hot flashes due to menopause.

It’s important to know that women who are pregnant should not take Lynkuet. Lynkuet can cause serious side effects, including central nervous system effects and daytime impairment. Don’t drive or do hazardous activities until these effects go away. Serious side effects also include increased liver blood test values, risk of pregnancy loss, and risk of seizure. The common side effects of Lynkuet include headache, fatigue, dizziness, feeling drowsy or sleepy, stomach (abdominal) pain, rash, diarrhea, and muscle spasms. Please refer to the full Important Safety Information below, and the Full Prescribing Information on Lynkuet.com/pi for more information. Women should speak with an HCP to determine if Lynkuet is right for them.

Here, Dr. Bitner shares what she feels women should know about moderate to severe hot flashes due to menopause—and how to prepare for and discuss treatment options with your doctor.

This interview has been lightly edited for clarity and concision.

Dr. Bitner: A hot flash is a sensation of warmth in the face, neck, and chest, or sudden intense feelings of heat and sweating. They can happen day and night. Hot flashes are one of the most common symptoms of menopause. They are considered mild when they involve a sensation of heat without sweating, moderate when there is a sensation of heat with sweating but you are able to continue activity, and severe when there’s a sensation of heat with sweating that causes you to be unable to continue activity.

Dr. Bitner: I’ve heard some women say that they think their hot flashes are something to just “get through.” I’ve also had many patients who say that their moderate to severe hot flashes can come on unexpectedly and they were surprised that hot flashes can last several years during menopause. Menopause is a phase that all women will go through at some point in their lives, and many women will experience moderate to severe hot flashes due to menopause. On average, moderate to severe hot flashes due to menopause last 3.6 years after diagnosis of menopause, though not all women will experience hot flashes for that period of time or even at all. Individual hot flashes can last anywhere from 1 to 5 minutes, and may occur a few times a week or several times per day or night. Understanding this can help women better understand their hot flashes due to menopause and start a conversation with their healthcare provider.

Dr. Bitner: Women may sometimes feel hesitant to bring up their experience with moderate to severe hot flashes with their healthcare provider. But this is a conversation worth having—particularly when moderate to severe hot flashes are their primary concern.

Something I’ve seen in my practice is that many women come in for a routine visit where there’s a lot to cover. They may not always mention their hot flashes during the visit, but that could be because they are trying to manage hot flashes on their own.

Fed Governor Christopher Waller questioned who bears responsibility for fraud, compromised keys and failed transactions as traditional financial assets move onto blockchains.

Speaking at The Clearing House’s annual conference in New York on Nov. 17, an event bringing together banking and payments industry leaders, Waller questioned who would bear responsibility when fraudsters exploit smart contracts, private keys are compromised, transfers go wrong or assets become stranded on failed blockchains.

Waller said the level of security and oversight required could depend on the importance of the financial transactions involved:

The expansion of tokenized finance would also require clear legal frameworks governing ownership rights, custody and settlement, he said, arguing that governance and legal protections are as important as technical safeguards in building trust.

Waller’s remarks came as four Democratic senators pressed the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) over safeguards for tokenized stocks. In a letter released Monday, the lawmakers questioned who would be responsible for shares transferred outside regulated platforms and whether regulators could freeze or recover the tokens.

Related: Custodia Bank loses Supreme Court bid for direct Fed payment access

Waller wasn’t the only Federal Reserve governor to raise concerns about emerging financial technologies this week. His remarks followed a Monday speech by fellow Fed Governor Michael Barr, who warned that artificial intelligence could introduce new cybersecurity risks as financial institutions increasingly adopt the technology.

Barr said AI-enabled attackers were exploiting vulnerabilities previously considered too difficult to target, while autonomous AI systems could behave in ways that undermine security controls

“Attackers only need to be right once, while defenders need to be right all the time,” Barr said.

#4874. Ethereum Devs Weigh a Scaling Upgrade That Could Break 15,000 Apps

Ethereum Devs Weigh a Scaling Upgrade That Could Break 15,000 Apps

Ethereum’s upcoming Glamsterdam upgrade threatens to break as many as 15,000 smart contracts, developers warned during a core developer call Monday, forcing a debate over how much disruption the network should tolerate in the name of scaling.

The concern centers on two proposed changes, EIP-8037 and EIP-8038, designed to let Ethereum scale from 60 million gas to as much as 200 million gas per block, a roughly 3.3x jump that developers say would sharply lower costs for most users while keeping state growth in check.

The problem, flagged late in the development process, is that the changes break certain invariants, assumptions that some smart contracts were built to rely on.

“Multiple contracts were relying on invariants in the protocol that are modified by 8037 and 8038,” said Marius van der Wijden, an Ethereum Foundation developer who worked on the scaling effort.

He acknowledged that the team “wanted to do significant public outreach” but that timelines slipped amid reorganizations and budget cuts at the foundation. He said he shares “a lot of blame” as the last remaining scaling lead still at the EF.

Two security firms, ChainSecurity and Dedaub, presented findings from AI-assisted audits, with the combined search turning up roughly 200 distinct classes of affected contracts, most tied to gas-cost increases rather than the new mechanics themselves.

Van der Wijden put the highest estimate at 10,000 to 15,000 contracts, a “fringe subset” of Ethereum’s roughly 90 million, with impacted value he loosely pegged in the low hundreds of thousands of dollars among contracts not yet committed to upgrading.

App developers pushed back on the framing. Jango, who builds the Juicebox protocol, warned the change undermines “composability,” a core Ethereum value prop, and shakes “developer confidence in building immutable protocols.” A Uniswap developer urged that EIP-8037 “should definitely be reconsidered.”

The Ethereum Foundation already delayed Glamsterdam’s testnet fork over these gas-related security flaws. Developers stressed Monday that no decision has been made, with the question headed to Thursday’s execution-layer call.

But several signaled a strong desire to ship the fork as planned, arguing that removing the changes could delay Glamsterdam, and the broader roadmap toward post-quantum security, by four to six months, time they say Ethereum can’t spare as quantum and AI threats loom.

#4873. Want to Turn Back the Clock? These 10 Diets May Help You Age Better

You’ve got way more options than just the Mediterranean diet.

When healthy aging is the goal, it makes sense to try everything you can to make it happen. That means doing your best to exercise regularly, keep up with doctor's appointments, and eat a well-balanced diet. You have lots of options when it comes to the last one—but it can be hard to know which of the many popular eating plans is right for you. Thankfully, new research has helped narrow the choices.

The study, which was published in Nature Communications, analyzed several different diets to see how they impacted biological aging. (Biological aging is the age of your cells, while your chronological age is how old you are.) Popular eating plans like the Mediterranean diet and the DASH (Dietary Approaches to Stop Hypertension) diet made the cut, of course, but several lesser-known diets did too. Here’s what to know.

Meet the experts: Jessica Cording, RD, author of The Little Book of Game-Changers; Keri Gans, RD, author of The Small Change Diet; and Sonya Angelone, RD, PhD, a former spokeswoman for the Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics and a San Francisco-based dietitian.

For the study, researchers analyzed data from 6,470 participants who were 30 and older. Researchers looked at some of the participants' biomarkers that correlated with biological age and compared that with information about their diets.

After analyzing the data, researchers found that healthier eating in general was linked with slower biological aging, no matter which diet people chose. Each specific eating plan offered an edge with certain perks, though. Case in point: The DASH diet (which is specifically meant to stop hypertension) had more cardiovascular benefits for biological aging, while the MIND diet (which combines the Mediterranean and DASH diets for brain health) offered cognitive perks. But researchers discovered that there were a lot of shared biological aging benefits between the different types of diets.

These are the 10 diets flagged as being good for biological aging:

All of these diets are slightly different, but there are a few common threads. "They generally emphasize fruits, vegetables, whole grains, and other nutrient-dense foods," says Keri Gans, RD, author of The Small Change Diet.

The diets also stress the importance of minimally processed foods, while limiting refined carbs, added sugars, and processed meats, according to Sonya Angelone, RD, PhD, a former spokeswoman for the Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics and a San Francisco-based dietitian. "The recommended foods provide fiber, antioxidants, polyphenols, vitamins, minerals, and healthy fats that support metabolic health and help protect cells from oxidative stress and chronic inflammation," she says. Oxidative stress and chronic inflammation are both linked to a higher risk of disease, Angelone points out.

These diets also support the heart, brain, and digestive systems, says Jessica Cording, RD, author of The Little Book of Game-Changers. "All of these things factor into the aging process and somebody's quality of life as they age," she says. "When you're eating to support these different organ systems, you support your longevity and lower your risk of disease."

There are a few things to take away from the findings, according to dietitians. One is that there isn't a single eating plan that's superior to others when it comes to longevity. "It's the overall quality of what we eat consistently that matters most, rather than following a particular diet or avoiding individual foods," Gans says.

While there are plenty of diet plans out there that claim they can help you live longer, Angelone stresses this: "Healthy aging doesn’t have to include expensive foods, supplements, or restrictive diets."

Finally, the study underscores the power of nutrition in keeping you healthy. "Our genes are not our destiny," Angelone says. "We can change the expression of our genes—genomics—with nutrition and lifestyle habits."

Supporting healthy aging with the way you eat means giving your body the fuel it requires to function well, Angelone says. "Healthy aging isn’t about finding a perfect diet or miracle food or supplement," she says. "It is about consistently providing foods that supply nutrients needed by our bodies to function optimally, repair cellular damage, and protect themselves. This will impact how we age."

#4872. Cathie Wood's ARK Sells $85 Million in Nvidia, Buys $40 Million in Crypto Stocks

Cathie Wood's ARK Sells $85 Million in Nvidia, Buys $40 Million in Crypto Stocks

Cathie Wood's ARK Invest sold roughly $85 million worth of Nvidia shares Monday while buying close to $40 million in crypto-exposed stocks, rebalancing exposure to technology and fintech stocks during a broad selloff.

The firm's daily trade file for November 16 shows sales of 543,092 Nvidia shares across two actively managed exchange-traded funds. Using Monday's $156.14 closing price, those shares were worth approximately $84.8 million; the disclosures list share counts rather than the exact prices ARK received.

ARK bought 277,523 shares of payments company Block, worth about $23 million at the close. It also added 180,534 shares of stablecoin issuer Circle, valued at $10.4 million, and 53,760 shares of crypto exchange Coinbase, worth around $6.4 million.

The purchases were spread across funds rather than concentrated in one vehicle. ARK's flagship Innovation ETF (ARKK) bought Circle and most of the Block shares, while its Next Generation Internet ETF (ARKW) bought Coinbase and the remaining Block stock.

All three crypto-linked stocks fell Monday. Circle dropped 7.3%, Coinbase declined 6.1% and Block lost 1.9%, while Nvidia slid 4.1% as investors continued selling technology shares.

That makes the whole movement seem like a shift in holdings, not evidence that ARK expects cryptocurrencies to recover before AI stocks. The manager says its funds can rebalance every trading day, and its trade notifications don't disclose why each position was changed or establish that particular sales financed particular purchases.

ARK had bought 90,443 Nvidia shares just one week earlier, on November 9, during another selloff. The latest sale therefore reverses some of that buying without necessarily suggesting the firm has abandoned the chipmaker or its long-standing investment case for artificial intelligence.

ARK also purchased 378,515 shares of SpaceX, worth roughly $52 million, while selling 30,659 shares of crypto exchange Bullish and units of Ethereum and Solana staking funds. So in this case, Wood would be selling crypto to buy one single AI stock.

Those sales included 300,000 shares of the 3iQ Ethereum Staking ETF and 350,000 shares of the 3iQ Solana Staking ETF. The firm's buying of crypto companies coincided with cuts to other crypto-related investments, a distinction that matters when trying to read a trading strategy from one day's activity.

Wood has repeatedly bought companies that handle crypto trading and payments during market selloffs. In September, ARK bought $37 million in Block stock in one session, and it previously increased its Circle and Coinbase stakes while reducing exposure to other crypto names.

The companies offer different ways to invest in digital assets without holding tokens directly. Block runs Cash App and Bitcoin-related products; Circle issues the USDC dollar-backed stablecoin; and Coinbase, the only American crypto exchange listed on the stock market, earns revenue from cryptocurrency trading and other services.

ARK's strategy has never been a simple choice between crypto and AI. Its flagship fund already counted Circle, Coinbase and SpaceX among major positions in August, alongside businesses tied to artificial intelligence and financial technology, as earlier holdings showed.

Nvidia's leadership changed five days before Monday's trades. Co-founder Jensen Huang resigned as CEO on November 11, with finance chief Colette Kress appointed interim chief executive, according to the company's SEC filing.

The chipmaker is due to report fiscal third-quarter results after the market closes Tuesday, with a conference call at 5 p.m. Eastern. Those results will give investors their first earnings update since the leadership change—one day after ARK sold more than half a million shares.

#4871. Lighter incident exposes risks beyond withdrawal controls

Crypto platforms need enforceable limits on every route an API key can use to transfer value, including trades, internal transfers and shared pools.

A recent incident where over $10 million was siphoned out of a decentralized perpetual futures exchange shows the shortcomings of focusing security on withdrawal controls

According to Lighter’s postmortem, an attacker used compromised API keys to move funds into a public pool and redeem shares held through another account. Bitquery traced a withdrawal of 10.39 million USDC. The exchange said its protocol and smart contracts were unaffected.

Lighter now requires wallet signatures for transfers into public pools and has made API-key signatures non-public. It also plans IP allowlists and configurable permissions for individual keys.

Lighter has since restored deposits and withdrawals while also returning about $5 million in USDC (USDC) to the affected trader.

Lighter incident infographic. Source: Bitquery

The incident highlights how cybersecurity reviews need to look past smart contract vulnerabilities. It is important to also consider the gap between the permissions a system grants and the financial consequences those permissions allow.

Related: Google says hackers use AI agents to find and exploit software flaws

The real risk involving a credential depends on the balances it can reach, the transactions it can initiate and the exposures it can create. Whether it is permitted to withdraw assets and to which destinations are just two of many factors. As Lighter put it in its postmortem:

This means that a user needs to establish a clear mandate for each credential. The mandate can specify accessible accounts, permitted markets, order sizes, pricing tolerances and aggregate exposure. Moving capital into a shared pool or expanding those limits can require separate authorization.

The same logic applies to additional signatures. A second signature adds meaningful protection when its approval process independently evaluates the transaction’s financial effect.

#4870. How to Lose Weight Naturally, According to Experts

Here are 10 easy-to-follow tips to speed up the process—and make it more enjoyable.

Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

Starting a weight-loss journey is no easy feat. There’s a lot to think about, between getting into a regular workout routine, changing up what you eat, and maybe even considering a GLP-1 medication.

But at its core, weight loss is about developing a healthy, sustainable relationship with food and movement. You don’t have to make a dozen changes all at once—the goal is long-term success, even if it’s a slow process. That’s why you should aim to lose one to two pounds a week, says Danielle Crumble Smith, RDN, a dietitian at Eat Well, Live Well. Working out at a manageable pace, eating balanced meals, and making maintainable changes can help you feel your best.

Meet the experts: Danielle Crumble Smith, RDN, is a nutritionist at Eat Well, Live Well. Kami Blease, CPT, is a personal trainer at Fyt Personal Training. Tatyana Johnston, CPT, is a former Nike master trainer and event specialist at Lululemon. Jordan Hill, RD, is a nutritionist with Top Nutrition Coaching.

Ahead, experts share their 10 best tips to make your weight-loss journey successful.

First, be sure to consult your doctor—they’ll help you set mindful, attainable goals that will keep your body healthy and strong. Then, try implementing more of these habits into your lifestyle:

Take the stairs every day at work or hold a quick plank first thing in the morning. "All these things add up over time," says Kami Blease, CPT, a personal trainer at Fyt Personal Training. "I recommend finding things you could do almost daily.”

Additionally, try adding a brisk 30-minute walk into your day (even if it’s broken up into three 10-minute walks) to increase calorie burn and push you closer to your weight-loss goals, per the Mayo Clinic. "It's low impact and not a super strenuous form of movement, which increases the chances that someone will stick with it,” says Tatyana Johnston, CPT, a former Nike master trainer and event specialist at Lululemon. "Just remember to recover with hydration, fuel, and stretching.”

Burn fat and build muscle with the WH+ 4-week walking plan

Strength training “helps with balance and stability, improves metabolism, and even lowers your risk of certain diseases," says Blease. Resistance training has also been found to help with weight loss and body recomposition, according to a 2026 study in Frontiers in Endocrinology that had 304 adults follow a calorie-restricted diet and either resistance train, do aerobic exercise, or no exercise for 1 to 18 months.

To get comfortable with form, try practicing bodyweight exercises first, Blease recommends, then add weights after you’ve mastered the move. This can help you focus on progressive overload—which means gradually increasing the weight, frequency, or number of reps over time, Blease says. Eventually, you should aim to work all major muscle groups at least twice a week, per the new ACSM resistance training guidelines.

Cardio can also help with weight loss—the CDC recommends 150 minutes of moderate-intensity aerobic activity (such as brisk walking) per week, or 75 minutes of vigorous-intensity activity (like running) each week. However, this number can vary based on someone’s individual health, and the intensity of the cardio. "Consistency is key. If you can establish and stick to a cardio schedule, you have a better chance at losing weight and keeping it off," Johnston says. Playing sports, working out with friends, or listening to a podcast during cardio can help boost your motivation too.

Also, if you enjoy high-impact exercises and want to lose weight fast, HIIT workouts can be a great way to expend a lot of energy in a short period of time. "You can ramp up the intensity by trying to get in more reps during a certain amount of time or using heavier weights while maintaining the same time goal,” says Blease. “Both will increase your intensity and continue to challenge your body."

If the gym or workout classes aren’t really your speed, choose a form of movement that you love so you can stay consistent with it. “Hiking, swimming, skiing, surfing, or biking are all forms of movement that might feel more sustainable,” says Blease.

"Start smaller than you might think," Blease says. "Often, people overcommit because they are excited. However, it's then easy to get burnt out." After a few weeks, add in a second day, and when that feels seamless, try a third, and over time, you'll find a cadence that works for you, she adds.

Just make sure you always have at least one rest day. "People can get so fixated on weight loss that they end up [overdoing exercise and] hurting themselves," Blease says. "Take time to stretch, rest, and recover as needed."

"Having a trainer create a program that is specific to your needs ensures that you are more likely to get the results you are looking for—and keep your body safe in the process," says Blease. They can help you lose fat while building muscle, which can better your overall metabolic health and insulin sensitivity, and regulate blood sugar to support a healthier body recomposition.

A trainer will also make sure you maintain proper form and that you stay consistent. Decide on a number of days per week that fits your goal and budget, and ask your trainer to help hold you accountable, Blease says.

Research suggests that working with a personal trainer may have more profound effects on weight loss: A 2024 study in Heliyon had 66 adults train individually, with a partner, or a personal trainer over 12 weeks, and they monitored their improvements in bench presses, squats, skeletal muscle mass, and fat mass. The group that worked with a personal trainer improved their leg training and reduced fat mass compared to the other groups.

Protein can help you stay full throughout the day, stabilize your blood sugar levels, and synthesize muscle mass, Smith says, helping with weight loss. While individual dietary needs vary, you can generally aim for 30 to 35 grams of protein per meal to help you stay full throughout the day. Some good sources include eggs, poultry, seafood, red meat, beans, peas, lentils, legumes, nuts, seeds, and soy, per the current Dietary Guidelines for Americans.

Additionally, "fiber is more slowly digested and helps keep you feeling full for a longer period,” Smith adds, recommending vegetables. Increased vegetable intake is also linked to lower blood sugar levels, lower triglycerides, and can help promote liver function. If you don't love veggies, you can also puree them and add them to a sauce or weight-loss-friendly smoothie.

Lastly, don’t forget about healthy (unsaturated) fats—which can help provide energy, per the Mayo Clinic. Try avocados, extra-virgin olive oil, nuts, seeds, soybeans, and seafood.

"Drinking enough water can help you to feel full and prevent overeating," says dietitian Jordan Hill, RD. Aim to drink about half your body weight in ounces of hydrating fluids per day.

Also, avoid sugary beverages. "Juices, sodas, and fancy coffees are often the calorie-equivalent of a meal, yet they will still leave you hungry," says Smith. "The sugar content is often more than a candy bar, which will cause blood sugar levels to rise." Instead, replace your beverages with fruit-infused water, herbal tea, or coffee with cinnamon or zero-calorie sweeteners.

Avoid foods that are high in added sugars, unhealthy fats, and empty calories, which can contribute to weight gain, says Hill: "Instead, focus on eating whole, nutrient-dense foods that will provide your body with the nutrients it needs."

Listening to your internal cues of hunger and fullness can help you control portion sizes, which can also aid weight loss. "Honoring fullness can help prevent overeating and ensure that you're not consuming more calories than your body needs," says Hill. Keeping a food journal can also help you become more mindful of what you're eating, when, and how you're feeling throughout the process of losing weight.

“When you skip meals or go too long in between meals or snacks, you get overly hungry. This makes it much more difficult to make healthy choices, and it also makes it harder to not overeat later," says Smith. Skipping meals can also result in a slower metabolism and leave you feeling fatigued, which can negatively impact your workouts both in effort and recovery.

If you struggle to eat consistent meals, Smith recommends munching on small snacks throughout the day. “Set yourself up for success by bringing healthy snacks with you when you’re away from home, so you’re not caught in a situation where you are really hungry but have no access to healthy food,” she says.

If you need extra assistance, a dietitian can analyze your diet and recommend personalized tips for how you can eat to lose weight, which may be more helpful than doing it on your own. A 2025 review of articles on weight-loss interventions provided by a dietitian for overweight and obese adults in the Journal of the Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics looked at how working with a dietitian improved their health markers, as opposed to not working with one (the control group). The group that worked with a dietitian had improved weight loss, waist circumference, blood pressure, and quality of life compared to the control group.

When you encounter a setback (like when you skip a few days of workouts), it can be discouraging and all-consuming, and can cause you to fall off track. "One of the most crucial components of successfully reaching a goal is to not let setbacks ruin our progress,” says Johnston. “The setback is often not as severe as we think, and will not impact our end goal very much at all.”

Just take a breath and realize we’re all human and mistakes are normal; then move forward with your health plan in mind.

And don’t forget to be kind to yourself. Practicing self-compassion and returning to your plan will help reinforce your goal and remind you that this weight-loss journey requires patience and perseverance. "Practice giving yourself grace when [you] slip up,” Johnston says. “As long as it doesn’t become a habit, you will continue moving forward towards your goal.”

#4869. What “Food Is Medicine” Actually Means, According to a Cardiologist

Plus, Chef Marcus Samuelsson shares easy ways to sneak more plant-based foods into your diet.

Despite what fitfluencers and gym bros might have you believe, eating healthy is about a lot more than counting macros and calories. Every day, scientists are learning more about how our eating habits can influence health beyond just our weight, including blood pressure, cholesterol, blood sugar, and risk of developing heart disease.

That's part of the idea behind a buzzy approach to health care known as “food is medicine,” which contends that what we put on our plates can be a meaningful part of preventing and managing disease.

The challenge is understanding what actually helps and turning that knowledge into meals we want to keep eating. To unpack this, Future You host and editorial director of Men’s and Women’s Health Rich Dorment sits down with Marcus Samuelsson, the acclaimed restaurateur and author of the new cookbook, Back to Green, and Louai Razzouk, MD, a cardiologist at NYU Langone Health.

Here’s a look at some of the themes covered in the episode:

Samuelsson says that beso is an Ethiopian drink that combines roasted barley with water or milk of your choice. “You just shake it and this is the best protein shake you can have,” he says. You can find the more specific recipe in Back to Green.

He grew up eating foods like beso as well as shiro, a stew made from chickpea flour, and other Ethiopian “superfoods” that he incorporates into his dishes today.

Dr. Razzouk says it doesn't mean that you can treat a disease with food alone. “It does mean that you may be able to prevent it by having a healthier and more balanced diet, and possibly minimize how many medications you need to be on,” he says.

Dr. Razzouk says that while you may still need to be on medication, food can make a “huge” impact when it comes to managing conditions like diabetes or high cholesterol. “Food impacts our level of inflammation, our insulin sensitivity, our weight,” and our blood pressure, he says.

The first warning sign that a patient’s diet may be less than ideal is if they get most of their food from Uber Eats or another delivery service. “Most of the stuff that we order in, especially living in New York City, contains a lot of saturated fats, a lot of added salt, and a lot of processed food,” he says. He discusses a couple more red flags in the episode, including meal timing.

In his early 20s, traveling in Southeast Asia and Singapore opened his eyes to a new way of eating—and the idea that there’s great food to be found all over the world.

A plant-forward diet doesn't have to exclude animal protein, he says, pointing to the Mediterranean and DASH diets as examples of eating plans that incorporate some meat. “What I tell patients is that typically if you have a choice between getting a source of protein from an animal source versus from plants, then I would try to get it from plants,” he says.

“What I tell patients is that I want you to enjoy your life,” Dr. Razzouk says, adding that fad diets typically don’t work. “What we would like you to do is find a balance,” he says, eating in a way that's enjoyable and that benefits your health.

It's a lentil salad with a coconut turmeric vinaigrette—and Samuelsson breaks down why the flavors work so well together, plus ingredients you may have in the fridge or pantry that can level it up even further.

He’ll often bring home new ingredients (e.g. spirulina) and encourage his son to look up the health benefits before they cook with it together.

Dr. Razzouk says diets high in fiber not only may lower your risk of colon cancer, but they also may lower your level of LDL cholesterol and triglycerides, which impact your risk of cardiovascular disease. It also helps keep you full.

Cooking together can be an enjoyable family activity, Samuelsson says. “When I cook waffles and pancakes with my kids, we have fun,” he says. “The kitchen is a mess, but iPads are down, we're spending time together.”

Samuelsson suggests chickpeas, sea moss, and the fruit soursop. Dr. Razzouk suggests nuts (walnuts in particular) and extra-virgin olive oil.

LifeStraw then packed its filter inside the stainless steel bottle, which we found to be much more appealing than plastic models where you can see the filter inside.

The cost of the Lifestraw Go here is a little elevated, but you are paying for the special filter. You do need to change the LifeStraw filter inside about every 60 days, so that's an extra cost. The payoff though, from what our editors discovered, is the peace of mind you get filling up your water bottle at a public water fountain or from tap water that comes out of a sink.

Grab this water bottle if you're looking for a filtered option with excellent design. There are times when you can’t fully trust your water source but this vessel affords peace of mind (and no bickering of the gut).

To say these bottles were tested is an understatement. Over the course of several years, various Men's Health editors and I put them to work—like, overtime. We paired them up with the most active members of our team, allowing us to get a clean picture of just how well these bottles perform. Hot weather, cold weather, in the gym, out on the trail, on the saddle of a bike, on plane rides, or just commuting; we brought them everywhere.

Throughout the process, we paid close attention to various attributes. Obviously, we wanted a water bottle that looks good. But more importantly, we wanted a water bottle that made staying hydrated easy, thoughtless, and perhaps even enjoyable. We analyzed design, material, size, and special features. We waded through reputable reviews and talked up insiders in the outdoors recreation and sporting worlds for their takes. And of course, we looked at price.

In the end, the Yeti has won us over on all fronts. Durable, lightweight, packable, and super affordable, it has been a favorite among many testers since it released in 2022. But several others came close, offering different traits like filtration, improved insulation, or more sophisticated lids.

Some people prefer wide-mouth tops on their water bottles for faster drinking, while others prefer a spout design that's much smaller and easier to sip. Really it comes down to preference, but there are spout designs we tested that are more enjoyable to drink from than others. Do keep in mind that lots of companies make tops that are interchangeable in case you want to switch to a different design.

To avoid any contamination of plastics, most water bottles we reviewed came in a metal design. There are some plastic water bottles we tested, however, that were BPA-free and we found to not have any impact on taste. Our top-tested water bottle from Yeti is actually made from BPA-free plastic. Our editors have tested this water bottle for nearly two years and have found no issues with taste or with material breakdown from a dishwasher.

Material also dictates temperature retention, with things like double-insulated stainless steel keeping things nice and chilled for long periods of time. Plastic tends to not insulate quite as well, but can be quite durable (and recycled). Keep this in mind as you weigh how important an ice-cold pull of water is to you.

How much water are you going to need? Capacity is a vital consideration, as you might just be looking for a little hydration while at work (where you can continue to refill when necessary) or be out and about all weekend at the campground, potentially away from a water source. Less volume is just fine for quicker outings or when you want to be streamlined, like on a bike. But you'll be wanting additional capacity for, say, lengthy conferences, road trips, or exhausting workout routines.

There are a few water bottles we selected thanks to special features our editors love. Lifestraw, for example, provides some of the best water filtration you can buy. The fact Lifestraw discreetly hides its filter behind a stainless steel body is a huge reason why we featured it on our list. The same goes for the Camelbak Podium, as its insulated body and cap and spout design make it especially suitable for indoor gym settings.

Yes. A reusable bottle is easier on the planet for that very reason—it's reusable. Single-use plastic is wasteful stuff and, worse, it does not decompose, likely ending up in the ocean and your food supply chain (not to mention turning into microplastic). Going with a bottle like the ones listed here does require some energy and inputs upfront, but because it's your long-term bottle (don't go losing it now), the carbon footprint is less.

You can take it a step further by purchasing a bottle made with responsibly sourced materials, sometimes even made from up-cycled or recycled materials. Look for non-BPA (a bad chemical) options and preferably ones that use very little if no plastic. Glass and stainless steel are generally easier on Mother Earth. And be good to yourself by keeping the thing clean and sterile.

Here's the thing about mold: It likes wet environments. You know, like inside of your water bottle. It's a repulsive thought, but some of that gunk buildup in your vessel might just be mold. Don't fret, you can clean the thing.

Now, it would take a fair amount of mold to sicken the average person but regardless, a clean water bottle is just worth having. Wash your bottle daily, either in the dishwasher if it's permitted or by hand, ideally with hot water and a scrub to get into those nooks and crannies—water bottle brushes are a great tool.

Occasionally, consider a more intense clean. Do to the bottle as you might to your coffee maker, soaking it in a mix of vinegar and water. Even the occasional boiling water soak will help keep the bottle pristine.

#4866. The Healing Power of a Post-Divorce ‘Hoe Phase’

Many women use celibacy to process and move on from a breakup, but what if casual sex is the antidote they need instead?

Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

Zion* was little more than a stranger when he lifted me up onto his lap in one swift movement. His hands were sure, yet soft, as he held my face, kissing me deeply. After a few moments, I pulled back, then looked down, unsure of how to respond to what I could feel was his obvious desire for sex.

I wanted him. But I was afraid I didn’t know how to do this.

Zion was the second man I’d been with since my divorce, but he was the first one I actually liked—and that I wanted to like me back.

Sensing my insecurity, Zion tipped my chin to his mouth and kissed me softer. With my legs wrapped around his waist, he picked me up and carried me to his bedroom. I threw my head back, curls wild, and giggled in a way I hadn’t in over a decade of being married.

As our bodies tangled together, our breathing synced, he looked me directly in the eyes and asked, “Are you ok? How does this feel?” I had never had a man check in with me like that.

“I feel so safe with you,” I whispered into Zion’s ear. It surprised me to know how true that was since we’d only met a few hours ago. I’d been sitting alone at a bar, as had he, and we’d struck up a casual conversation that quickly turned intimate.

I hadn’t felt safe in a long time. Not since sex with my ex-husband had become less like something I looked forward to each week and more like a duty I dreaded.

Throughout our 13-year marriage, I felt like I had expectations placed on me and my body as a wife—my husband’s “needs” often seemed to supersede my own. Consent felt implied. I didn’t think I could say “no” because that might be met with anger or coercive tactics, like begging me over and over until I relented. Each time, my sense of safety and trust eroded.

Eventually, I started recoiling from my husband’s touch because it felt like every hug or little neck rub would turn into him wanting sex.

Naturally, my libido took a nosedive. I thought the problem was me, so I went to sex therapy. But as I started to explore myself in those sessions, I realized I was still sexual. In fact, I was highly sexual. I just didn’t want to have sex with him because I always felt hypervigilant for my emotional and physical safety.

After two months of sex therapy, I asked my ex to sleep in a separate bedroom. Then, I asked for the separation that led to our divorce.

In the early stages of my separation, I was tempted to swear off sex—and men—entirely. This is not uncommon, says Laura Sgro, LCSW, an anxiety and trauma therapist in Los Angeles. “Many women are like ‘screw men,’ because it’s a fear-based response,” she explains. “They’ve learned over time, especially in long-term marriages, to associate sex and intimacy with something that’s not going to be pleasurable for them, with something that’s not really their choice.”

Additionally, love and relationship coaches on social media often suggest celibacy as a way to heal after divorce and sexual trauma. But what if casual sex is the antidote many women need instead?

Once the stress of the divorce dissipated and I settled into my new life as a single mother, I just wanted to have some fun. So, I started leaving my house more often, instead of being wrapped up in “mom duties” all of the time. I went to cute cafes to work, had lunch or drinks at a bar, smiled at men who looked at me, and started conversations with people around me. That’s how I met Zion, and, well, one thing led to another…

Although I liked him—immediately—I wasn’t looking for commitment. Being someone’s partner or girlfriend didn’t sound appealing to me because I’d just escaped all the oppressive gendered expectations that had come with those labels. I just wanted to feel desired and have sex again—uninhibited, no strings attached, exploratory, and pleasurable. I wanted to be free.

Casual sex can be a way for women to take their agency back, says Alica Livingston, a licensed marriage and family therapist based in Texas. “When sex becomes their choice—who they have sex with, when they have sex, what that sex looks like—it can be an incredibly healing and powerful experience.”

It can also be an informative one. Many women don’t know what they like in the bedroom because so much of their sexual experience has been framed around their partner’s pleasure, says Sgro. Embracing casual sex after a breakup or divorce can help women center their own pleasure and regain their confidence.

But if you want to get to know your body better before jumping into bed with someone new, try some solo exploration. “Experimenting with self-touch, even non-sexually, can help women identify what they actually like and dislike,” says Sgro. She suggests touching yourself in ways you haven't tried before—light, firm, slow, still—and rate sensations as pleasant, neutral, or not for you. (For example, you might enjoy gently trailing your finger along the inside of your forearm, but want a firmer touch around your erogenous zones.) Over time, this self-exploration can expand into more sensual territory, like trying toys that offer different sensations or inviting a partner to explore further.

Sgro also recommends women find a hobby or activity that helps them connect with their bodies. “Many women feel disconnected from their bodies post-divorce, and it's so important to rebuild that connection with yourself on your terms,” she says. It can be yoga, weight lifting, dance classes—anything that helps you feel stronger, more empowered, and able to express yourself through movement.

For me, it was twerk classes. The rap music reminded me of the ’90s video vixens and my first “hoe phase” in high school. As a young woman, I had a lot of unsatisfying, performative sex out of pressure to be cool and feel chosen.

This, of course, is the argument against casual sex, and why embracing it often goes against the popular #BoySober and “decentering men” movements. These trends are not only a direct response to the violence women risk by romantically interacting with men; they are also evidence of the humiliating and lackluster dating dynamics we face now—breadcrumbing, micro-cheating, future faking, monkey branching (the Gen Z-informed list goes on).

It’s also true that more women than men experience postcoital dysphoria and regret after one-night stands, booty calls, and casual sexual encounters. But this isn’t just another case of the classic gender gap—it’s due to a variety of factors, not least of which is sexual satisfaction.

But casual sex that is intentional, focused on self-exploration, and re-centers your pleasure can take off the pressure to perform or please your partner, says Sgro.

Now that I was in my late 30s, I was determined that my second “hoe phase” would be all about me and what I wanted. For starters, I wrote down my “Hell Yes” and “Hell No” lists. It was an easy and straightforward way for me to figure out what I liked in bed, what I wanted to try, and what I wasn’t open to. I also used sexting to get more comfortable sharing my desires and boundaries with new partners, which was great practice for having those conversations in person.

For me, having a post-divorce “hoe phase” was exactly what I needed. I started having the best sex of my life, including with Zion. He was the first man I saw myself with post-divorce, but neither of us were ready for a commitment at the time, so our connection only lasted a few weeks. For the next three years, I entertained many casual romantic and sexual connections. Eventually, I realized that while having no-strings-attached sex was great, I love monogamy and would like to get married again. So, earlier this year, I started seriously dating someone else.

Unfortunately, it didn’t work out, and I recently became single again. Part of me wonders if I should have another “hoe phase”? Or, should I stay away from random men until I find my husband?

Sgro says any woman going through a divorce or a breakup should ask herself these kinds of questions—and be honest in her answers. “If you want casual sex, give yourself that permission to explore it in a way that feels good for you,” she says. “And if you’re not ready for that, that’s OK too. No one makes the rules except you.”

So, I don’t know if I’ll continue to embrace casual sex, take some time to explore celibacy, or perhaps return to a past romance. What I do know is that my “hoe phase” opened possibilities—for more autonomy and more pleasure. And maybe even love.

#4865. Bitcoin Investors Are Capitulating—That’s Historically Been a Bottom Signal

Bitcoin Investors Are Capitulating—That’s Historically Been a Bottom Signal

Bitcoin’s latest crash has pushed investors into the kind of loss-taking that has historically shown up near market bottoms.

Realized losses, which investors lock in when they sell coins for less than they paid, have climbed relative to the profits taken over the past year.

That measure now sits at levels seen only near the lows of 2018, 2020, 2022 and early 2023, according to a report published Tuesday by onchain analytics firm Glassnode. It’s the first such reading since then.

Most of the selling came from recent buyers. Holders of coins less than six months old took losses into early 2026, cashed in gains during the rally into September and October, and are now selling at a loss again, Glassnode said. Leverage has been flushed too, with Nov. 13 and 14 bringing some of the largest long liquidations relative to open interest since 2023.

Bitcoin fell to about $62,000 on Nov. 15 before bouncing, and it traded near $64,970 on Tuesday. More than $2 billion in liquidations over the weekend left traders watching $60,000 as a potential next stop, Decrypt reported. The slide deepened last week as fears of further Federal Reserve rate hikes erased Bitcoin’s summer rally. Rising interest rates generally do not bode well for risk assets like Bitcoin, since investors typically rotate to safer bets like U.S. Treasuries when rates elevate.

But there are early signs of support, according to Glassnode. Buyers absorbed about 66,000 BTC in the $62,000 to $66,000 range during the two days of heaviest selling, adding to a zone where recent buyers accumulated around the August low.

Resting bids on Binance and Coinbase within 5% of the price now outweigh asks by about 2.3 to 1. The Coinbase Premium, which compares Bitcoin’s price on Coinbase with global markets, briefly turned positive at the low as U.S. buyers stepped in.

Still, Glassnode stopped short of calling a bottom. Broad demand remains thin: stablecoin supply has shrunk 4.2% over 90 days, and the Coinbase Premium has slipped back to a small discount.

Meanwhile, U.S. spot Bitcoin ETFs extended their outflow streak to eight sessions on Monday and have bled about $2.2 billion so far in November, according to Decrypt’s ETF tracker.

That makes the $62,000 to $66,000 range the line to watch. Short-term holders bought very few coins below $62,000, and a large cluster of leveraged long positions sits just beneath it, between about $59,500 and $62,200.

A daily close below $62,000 could trigger a fast drop toward the June low of $58,500 and Bitcoin’s realized price of $53,700, the average price at which every coin last moved, Glassnode said.

On the upside, a move back above $74,100, the average cost basis of short-term holders, would confirm that a bottom is forming, according to the firm. Options traders on Deribit, meanwhile, price roughly a one-in-three chance that Bitcoin settles below $53,700 at the September 2027 expiry.

The Fed’s next rate decision is Dec. 9, a day before November inflation data is released.
