#4864. Eastern Europe crypto flows fall 7.9% as Ukraine draws $12B in stablecoins

Chainalysis found that Eastern Europe recorded the steepest decline in crypto activity of any region, while cross-border stablecoin transfers to Ukraine continued amid the ongoing war.

Eastern Europe recorded the steepest decline in cryptocurrency activity among the regions tracked by Chainalysis in the year ended June 2026, falling 7.9% even as retail-sized transfers increased in value, according to a report published Tuesday.

The region’s crypto economy shrank to $642.1 billion from $697.1 billion a year earlier, compared with a 1.6% decline globally, the report states. Russia, which accounted for roughly 44% of the regional total, saw activity fall 14.7% to $284.1 billion over the period. By contrast, Belarus recorded 27.6% growth, while Bulgaria, Moldova and Ukraine saw smaller increases.

The value of transfers of $10,000 or more to crypto services fell 17.4%, from $591.5 billion to $488.6 billion, according to the report.

The value of smaller transfers to crypto services, meanwhile, rose 8.3%. These retail-sized transfers accounted for 13.1% of the value sent to crypto services in Eastern Europe, the highest share of any region studied and above the global average of 10.1%.

Eastern European crypto activity by country, July 2025 to June 2026. Source: Chainalysis report

Crypto ATM activity also increased across Eastern Europe, with transaction volumes nearly doubling from $17.3 million to $33.9 million. Poland recorded a 120% increase in ATM transactions despite a 5% decline in centralized exchange activity, with stablecoins accounting for roughly 90% of its ATM transactions.

Chainalysis measures the crypto economy using inflows to crypto services, domestic transfers between personal wallets and cross-border inflows to personal wallets. The figures are measured in dollars, so cryptocurrency price changes can also affect the totals, according to its methodology.

Related: OpenPayd secures MiCA license as stablecoin adoption grows in Europe

Despite the broader regional decline, Ukraine remained a major destination for stablecoins, receiving $12 billion in cross-border wallet-to-wallet transfers. Of that, $2.41 billion was in retail-sized transfers below $10,000, according to Chainalysis.

Chainalysis also found that countries with larger Ukrainian populations, including prewar diaspora communities and refugees who arrived after Russia’s full-scale invasion in February 2022, generally sent more stablecoins to Ukraine. Among the 36 countries studied across Europe and North America,

Canada was the largest source of retail-sized, remittance-like transfers, at $359 million.

Crypto transfers to Ukraine by diaspora population, July 2025 to June 2026. Source: Chainalysis report

A Chainalysis spokesperson told Cointelegraph that the cross-border flows were largely denominated in US dollar-pegged stablecoins, although the firm did not provide a breakdown by individual token.

#4863. An Exercise Trampoline Can Make Cardio More Fun. These Are 6 We Like.

Experts share what makes a rebounder safe, comfortable, and worth adding to your routine.

Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

As a lifelong distance runner, I’ve had trouble finding low-impact cardio workouts that feel challenging enough when I’m not pounding the pavement. But that all changed when I discovered an exercise trampoline, also referred to as a rebounder. They use a similar style of trampoline to what you used to bounce around on as a kid in the backyard, just with a fitness twist. The result is that the sized-down versions are just as fun, but you also work up a sweat.

Using an exercise trampoline is known as rebounding, and this type of workout is considered a high-intensity movement that’s low impact. That sounds a little confusing, but it basically means using an exercise trampoline will get your heart rate up there while giving your joints a break, something that can be especially appealing for runners. If you’re like me and crave a challenging lower-impact workout that doesn’t include an exercise bike or rower, rebounding might be your new favorite cardio workout.

While rebounding workouts will get your heart rate up quickly, there are plenty of other health benefits to consider, too. A 2024 scientific review found that rebounding can be great for enhancing blood circulation, bone health, and balance. And a small, 2018 study of 18 women found that participants were able to lower their blood pressure and improve their VO2 max—a marker of cardiovascular fitness—on a 12-week rebounding program.

Outside of research studies, Nikki Gnozzio, CPT lists off rebounding benefits of better balance, overall strength, and, of course, more fun. That last part is worth considering, especially if you’ve been struggling with workout motivation or boredom.

Of course, you need a trampoline before you can try this out. According to the personal trainers we spoke with, a rebounder’s tension, adjustability, maximum weight, sturdiness, and size should all factor into your buying decision. Below are six options that stood out.

There are a lot of brands to choose from, but JumpSport stands out as one that’s stood the test of time. “JumpSport has been around since 1996 and is a well-respected brand,” says Melissa Cantillo, an ACE-certified personal trainer and fitness manager at Canyon Ranch. The brand’s mini trampoline line, which includes the JumpSport 530 Pro, popularized the bungee cord system that’s used in many exercise trampolines, she points out.

This trampoline uses 36 adjustable elastic cords for a quieter bounce, with seven firmness settings to help you find your ideal tension. It also uses 16-gauge steel tubing for durability, which is why you can use this trampoline inside or outside (just make sure you bring it back indoors after a good bouncing session to extend the life of your trampoline).

The JumpSport 530 Pro has an extension skirt to protect your feet in case you accidentally land on the cords. The legs are slightly arched at the top to lower the risk your trampoline will tip over. If space is a premium at your place, simply remove the legs and stash your trampoline in a closet or up against a wall to free up floor space.

Plenty of trampolines have features to help you break them down into a smaller size for storage. The Skybound Boogie Bounce Elite takes that even further, with a trampoline that folds in half like a taco and slides into an included carrying bag. The trampoline is relatively small to begin with—it has a 39-inch diameter—but that works in your favor when it comes to storage.

There’s a lot more to love about this trampoline, though. It has a built-in, adjustable handlebar for balance, which is especially handy given that smaller bouncing surface. The frame and skirt are already installed once it arrives, so you can simply snap in the legs and handlebar to get bouncing within minutes.

If you’re looking for workout guidance, you’ll appreciate the free one-month trial of the Boogie Bounce app. It shares more than 100 routines you can flip through. After that, it’s $4.99 a month.

The Stamina 36-inch Mini Trampoline has a petite enough size that won’t hog your workout space. It’s also just over $50, making it the most affordable option in our guide.

In addition to its smaller circumference, it has detachable rubber legs you can pop out to prop against a wall or slide under your bed. Taylor Beebe, CPT points out that the weight capacity is also a bit lower than the other models—250 pounds—but the whole thing collapses for convenience. She also praises the included Müüv app that offers trampoline workouts.This trampoline uses resistance bands instead of steel coils, which likely contributes to its lower weight limit. So, if you weigh more than 250 pounds, it’s best to look for a different model, like the Leaps & Bounds Rebounder. It also doesn’t have a handlebar for added stability, although the 49.5-inch model does.

Many fitness trampolines have removable legs, but some are easier to get on and off than others. While some require some serious muscle and maneuvering to get these in and out, the Leaps & Bounds Bungee Rebounder has legs that just screw into the bottom, creating a pretty flat, easy-to-store surface when you’re ready to stash it away.

This trampoline comes in your choice of 40- and 48-inch diameters. (This is the 40-inch model, but you can upgrade to the 48-inch option if you have the room for it.) The Bungee Rebounder uses adjustable elastic cords for quiet bouncing, along with a durable carbon steel frame.

Leaps & Bounds offers rare perks you won’t see with most other exercise trampoline brands: You can return this after 30 days if it’s not a good fit, and the trampoline comes with a lifetime warranty. While this is minor, it’s still worth mentioning: This trampoline comes in your choice of seven cord colors. Just be aware that if you want to tack on a stability bar, it will set you back an extra $93.

Exercise trampolines generally fall into a category known as rebounders or “mini trampolines,” which basically means they’re smaller than those massive ones kids use in backyards. But rebounders have a relatively small bouncing surface, so you have to be a little mindful about where you jump. The ACON Fit Hexagon Rebounder is 55 inches across, with a 40-inch bouncing surface, which is one of the largest you’ll find. That’s worth considering, whether you prefer a larger bouncing area or just want to build in some added insurance that you won’t accidentally rebound off.

This trampoline has a built-in handlebar that’s adjustable, in case you want extra help with balancing while you jump. The reinforced steel frame has six arched legs for stability. Keep in mind that the legs aren’t removable, just in case you want to store your trampoline in a closet or other smaller space.

The elastic cords allow for a quieter bouncing experience. (The trampoline comes with extra bungees in case one breaks.) This trampoline comes with a 10-year warranty on the frame and two-year coverage on the mat to help protect your investment.

The Sunny Health Springless trampoline delivers the basics at a relatively moderate price tag, making it ideal for those new to rebounding and still figuring out if it’s for them.

This trampoline has a less common square shape, which tends to provide a more consistent, uniform bounce across the entire mat. Since this trampoline is on the smaller side, that’s especially handy for small spaces. The smaller size and removable legs mean it won’t hog a lot of room at your place.

Another perk for beginners? The Sunny Health Springless comes with the free SunnyFit app, which includes rebounding workouts to get you started.

Tension is the tightness and level of resistance you’ll have on the trampoline as you jump. “Smaller exercise trampolines will be more resistant (have higher tension) because they sit closer to the ground, and you don’t want to be tapping the ground with each jump,” says Sydney Sherman, NASM-CPT. “They’re meant to absorb the shock as you land your jump, which is why they’re a great low-impact option for those of us with sensitive joints or coming back from an injury."

Some trampolines allow you to tweak the settings to better suit your needs. An adjustable handle is key (if your trampoline has a handle), Gnozzio says. But some will also allow you to adjust the tension to create a bouncier or less bouncy feeling.

The maximum weight limit for an exercise trampoline will be different based on how it is constructed or the brand. Generally, the weight limit often varies from 250 to 450 pounds. The sturdiness of an exercise trampoline will also vary, but you'll want to make sure it has rubber grip covers for the legs to stay in place (and not scrape your floors) and a handlebar that doesn't easily move for stability.

Sure, you’re already aware that your trampoline needs to fit in your room. But you need plenty of room around it, like a foot on either side, just to be safe. "A lot of trampoline workouts involve arm movements, so you’ll want to have space around you, as well as above you for jumping," says Gnozzio.

While you’re at it, don’t forget to factor in your ceiling height. A minimum 8-foot ceiling height is recommended, according to Cantillo. You don’t need to bounce in a room with an extra-high ceiling since you push into the trampoline more than you jump up, she explains. “Your feet may come off the trampoline anywhere from 1 inch to 8 inches depending on the workout,” Cantillo says.

We’ve continuously researched and updated our guide to the best exercise trampolines since we first published this story in 2021. To find the best exercise trampolines of 2026, we consulted with six personal trainers for their recommendations on elements to consider. We also got feedback from individual trampolines, taking careful note of the pros and cons of each. From there, we researched the most popular, top-rated exercise trampolines, stacking them up against expert feedback and advice. Only trampolines that met our strict criteria made the final guide.

#4862. Bunny Williams Never Set Out to Collect Birdhouses—Now a Whole Village of Them Stands in Her Connecticut Garden

Among the apple trees at the edge of AD100 Hall of Famer Bunny Williams’s storied country garden in Falls Village, Connecticut, stands a church with a sensible tin roof; a thatched cottage; a pagoda; a red house flying a tiny flag that she takes for a general store; and a shuttered confection that suggests a Russian dacha. Each is raised high on its own post, finished on every side, painted and weathered like the structures of a settled town—and none has a door you could fit a hand through. It is a hamlet fashioned for birds, assembled building by building, the way real towns often grow: slowly, and without a master plan.

For many years as Williams and her husband, the antiques dealer John Rosselli, combed fields and fairs for Treillage, the much-loved shop they ran in New York City until 2015, the birdhouses kept finding her. They gathered on shelves in the hayloft of her barn. “When I had two, I didn’t know what to do with them,” she says. “Then all of a sudden there were 10.” She decided they had been in storage long enough.

A farmhouse with a side porch crafted by the late Larry Smith, a North Georgia birdhouse builder known for fashioning charmingly detailed structures with metal roofs.

An A-frame house embellished with gingerbread trim and decorative brackets

Williams, on a tree stump next to the pagoda. The notch in the base of the birdhouse indicates that it was probably designed to be mounted on a roof.

At that point, Williams and Robert Reimer, head gardener on her property, started the process of reclaiming a long-overlooked point of land. To create space and liberate a stand of existing apple trees, they removed invasive species, then planted oat grass, bird-friendly scrub plants, and fruit-bearing pawpaw trees. To create the neighborhood, she had uniform posts made—tall, “so that you look up at them,” each wrapped with a metal band to deter ambitious squirrels from climbing too high and disturbing the tenants she had in mind. Finally, up went the houses, now totaling 17.

The attraction had nothing to do with value or pedigree. “Most of these birdhouses are sort of folk art,” she says. “They were somebody having fun building an unusual structure.” Not Monticello in miniature, not a replica of someone’s own house, just unknown makers, each with “an eye and a kind of humor,” none of them trying to be perfect. The proof is in the details: the gingerbread scallops on one many-holed high-rise (“somebody had a great time with their little saw”), the thatched-roof cottage she prizes because she has never seen another like it, the weather vane crowning the would-be dacha.

A church with a brick chimney, an oversized cupola, and Gothic Revival design elements.

A rare combination house and feeder that evokes a neoclassical temple

Williams calls this one the general store.

A colonial revival house with a columned portico built by Larry Smith

“It has a kind of Russian dacha feeling,” says Williams.

What she didn’t have was history—the dealers who sold them seldom had any to pass along. The record, it turns out, is often recoverable. “The period from 1890 to 1930 is really the birdhouse’s golden age,” says Jacob Torkelson, an architectural historian and researcher at the University of Pennsylvania’s Stuart Weitzman School of Design, and among the very few scholars in the country studying these objects, whose makers and manufacturers he has painstakingly been identifying, where a name survives. Across those decades, government pattern books encouraged farmers to install birdhouses to reduce pesticide use (the birds would eat the insects), while mail-order companies offered them to homeowners as pure whimsy, not to mention a way of promoting biodiversity in their gardens. Shown photographs of Williams’s collection, Torkelson supplied some of what the dealers couldn’t. He traced one house down to the catalog page: the six-room Bungalow Martin House sold by the E.F. Hodgson Company, which listed the model from about 1917 until the firm closed in 1944. “Birdhouses are these wonderful mirrors to the human condition,” Torkelson says. “They tell us the values that we have as a society or as individuals, in our houses, in our gardens.”

A double porch house also built by Larry Smith

This pagoda-inspired birdhouse provides multiple roosting spots.

An unusual thatched-roof cottage prized by Williams, who has never seen another like it.

Williams isn’t finished collecting. Last May at Trade Secrets, the annual Litchfield Hills garden fair she cofounded in 2001 to raise funds for a local nonprofit domestic violence support agency, she stopped at the tent of Jim Sidon, whose company, Sparrow 10:29, crafts avian-size replicas of real buildings. Sidon, based outside Atlanta, came to the work after retiring from the printing industry. His first architectural birdhouse, built in 2017, was a replica of the 1792 Federal-style mansion in Newburyport, Massachusetts, where he and his wife had rented two rooms as newlyweds. It was Sidon who recognized, in three of Williams’s houses, the hand of his late friend Larry Smith, a North Georgia birdhouse builder known for his metal roofs and charmingly rustic details. Williams has asked Sidon to build her something new, though she is still deciding exactly what. Unlike her anonymous makers, Sidon numbers and signs every house. “My hope is that years from now, someone’s searching that out,” he says, “and when they open it up, they’ll see my signature.”

A dovecote-inspired birdhouse offers multiple residences

A picturesque house topped with a prominent weather vane

Drawing the eye like miniature garden follies, the houses rise on poles amid a stand of apple trees from ground planted with oat grass and bird-friendly scrub plants.

In Falls Village, the upkeep routine is minimal: Every couple of years the houses come down, receive a coat of wood preservative, and go back up into the weather. Sidon’s constructions, with cedar exteriors and sealed against the elements, ask even less. His replica of the Newburyport house has stood in his own garden for nearly a decade untouched. “I just hose it off,” he says. None of this troubles Torkelson, a preservationist by training. “These houses were made to be ephemeral,” he says. “They weren’t made to last forever, and they should absolutely be used.”

As for the intended residents? Williams thinks the birds mostly prefer making their homes in the trees, where they carry on, she says, like a symphony orchestra: “I’ve always felt that one of the reasons they don’t live in these houses is the birds think it’s suburbia. But they like the atmosphere.” Come winter, when the woods go bare and the village shows through the branches, Sidon would bet the houses do get used, songbirds crowding in two and three at a time for warmth. Williams can’t say—she has never once climbed up to look. “If they are nesting,” she says, “I don’t want to bother them.”

#4861. World Bank Taps Circle and Citi to Test Stablecoins for Development Payments

World Bank Taps Circle and Citi to Test Stablecoins for Development Payments

The World Bank is turning to stablecoins to modernize how it moves development money, announcing Tuesday it will explore using Circle’s USDC and blockchain-based payment rails to speed up and cut the cost of disbursing funds around the world.

The institution said it will work with Citi and Circle to test how dollar-denominated, regulated stablecoins could operate alongside or improve its existing funds-distribution system, which runs on correspondent banking, the slow and costly network of intermediary banks that routes international payments.

Under the arrangement, Citi would supply its connections to established banking rails while Circle provides the infrastructure to mint and settle funds in USDC.

The logic is that even small efficiency gains, applied across the vast sums the World Bank moves, could free up meaningful resources for development. “This initiative is about exploring ways to make the financial plumbing of development work better for the people who need it most,” said World Bank Group President Ajay Banga, arguing that faster, cheaper money movement means “a health clinic gets built on time, a farmer gets paid before the harvest season ends.”

The effort builds on FundsChain, a World Bank blockchain platform designed to make fund disbursements more traceable. More than 350 projects across 96 countries are already onboarded to its digital ledgers, letting everyone involved in a project see how money is being spent.

The stablecoin exploration would focus initially on an intermediated, interoperable model, limited to borrower countries where digital assets are permitted, with plans to involve other banks over time.

Circle CEO Jeremy Allaire framed development finance as one of the most important applications for his company’s technology, saying money that moves “at the speed of the internet shouldn’t be reserved for the world’s biggest banks and corporations.”

Today, the @WorldBankGroup announced work with @circle and @Citi to bring the benefits of USDC to global funds distribution. A big step towards a more efficient and inclusive financial system.https://t.co/hq436tA5IR

— Jeremy Allaire (@jerallaire) November 17, 2026

Citi’s Shahmir Khaliq said the collaboration would deliver “24/7 capabilities at scale so that critical funds move in real time.”

The move hands the stablecoin industry a powerful institutional validator, and it fits a broader wave of traditional finance embracing the technology.

Wall Street is currently racing to claim the onchain dollar, with Goldman Sachs, Citi and other banks committing roughly $270 million to a joint stablecoin venture, while Deutsche Bank recently went live with crypto custody after a five-year buildout.

For Circle, whose USDC is the second-largest stablecoin, a role in the World Bank’s payment plumbing marks a notable step toward mainstream legitimacy, even as the broader crypto market endures a rough stretch of ETF outflows and falling prices.

Just in time for the last-minute holiday trips.

I’ve written extensively about sunscreen since 2019, most recently in our guide to SPF facts, spray sunscreen, and how one dermatologist uses it as a dry shampoo hack. But if you’re looking for a one-and-done power list of the best sunscreens of 2026, this is it.

And sunscreen’s benefits don’t stop there. Sun damage accumulates from daily activities like driving and sitting in front of a window, says dermatologist Hadley King, MD. That means even during the fall and winter, we should still double down on sunscreen. Here’s how to buy SPF like a dermatologist and beauty editor.

As a picky beauty editor, it really takes a lot for a product to truly impress me. The impressive ingredient list. Allow Dr. Goldenberg to explain. "Isdin's SPF contains ‘repairsomes,’ which help with reversing sun damage in skin cells," he says. That makes this a great pick for anyone with hyperpigmentation or sun spots, especially since the formula has a glowy, tinted finish.

I had a light sunburn last summer, and my dermatologist suggested I use this SPF. After I slathered on moisturizer and layered on this liquid sunscreen during the day, I noticed my skin was less red after just two days. I was floored because I hadn’t used any new products other than the Isdin Eryfotona Ageless. A year later, and I can confirm it’s still well worth using. My skin never breaks out, the lightweight formula absorbs quickly, and it’s water-resistant for active lifestyles. It’s also available in tinted and untinted options.

It absorbs in just a few minutes and mattifies my oily T-zone and leaves behind a soft, luminous finish. Not to mention, it doesn’t cause breakouts or irritate my skin when I’m dealing with seasonal changes and sensitivities.

If I had to be nitpicky, then the only thing I dislike about Isdin is the price. However, there’s a smaller 1.7 fl. oz bottle to help ease the pain. I’ll continue to repurchase this sunscreen because it works fabulously with my oily, acne-prone skin. It’s also helpful for my 50-something mom’s mature skin. I also converted our visual editor, Jason Speakman, into a fan—he noticed a decrease in facial redness over six months of daily use.

Neutrogena's sunscreen stick is a great product for those on the run, says Dr. Goldenberg. It's easy to apply or reapply, and it offers SPF 50 with water resistance, so people with active lifestyles really love it—just check the 10,208 perfect 5-star ratings on Amazon.

Neutrogena is cheap, travel-friendly, glides on clear, and is effective. However, we found it was too greasy for oily skin. However, if you have normal or dry skin, or just want to glow, this is the face sunscreen for you. With festival season underway, your skin will definitely “shine bright like a diamond” with the help of this sunscreen. And honestly, at just under $10, it’s worth trying.

Dr. Campbell is a fan of EltaMD's sunscreen, as are Lindsay Geller, Women's Health's lifestyle director, and Amanda Lucci, our special projects director. The line is a favorite of many dermatologists I consulted, and Dr. Ranella Hirsch, MD, highlights this particular sunscreen as her top pick. This is also Ritchey's new go-to. “As long as you don't smother yourself in it, I feel like it's pretty light for a sunscreen,” she says. “It's a little tacky after going on, but honestly, it was kind of nice—it definitely helped my makeup stick!” It also has a faint sunscreen smell, which she doesn't mind, since it reminds her that Anthelios Melt-In is working. Just keep in mind that a little goes a long way—a lesson Ritchey learned the hard way. “The first time I put too much in my hand, I looked like Larry the Lifeguard from SpongeBob SquarePants.”

Dermatologists advise applying two finger-lengths of sunscreen—about a quarter-sized amount—to your face and neck.

Tower 28 is one of the best sunscreens that I’ve ever used. It combines all of the benefits of a broad-spectrum mineral sunscreen with foundation-like coverage in 17 shades.

Knowing that richer sunscreen shades can be a real let-down, I hit up digital designer Taryn Colbert to give this one a whirl. The only downside? There is only one shade available: Translucent. It hasn’t left my caramel complexion looking ghostly. However, the brand makes other tinted powder sunscreens. Although it’s expensive, associate style and reviews editor Shannen Zitz has repurchased this sunscreen for over three years. She was so delighted with the results that she didn’t even apply concealer or setting powder. “I had to honestly do a double-take the first time that I was applying sunscreen and not makeup,” she says. “I would 100% recommend this product and will be a regular customer after this experience.”

Colbert was impressed by the lightweight texture but noted it required more effort to use. Notably, she had to wait for it to transform from white to her rich complexion before blending it onto her face. Colbert admits she had to work the sunscreen into her skin to ensure it didn’t look streaky, and that she didn’t miss any spots while waiting for the color to change. Still, she appreciates the overall appearance it left on her complexion. While not her perfect shade match, rich does resemble how her skin looks after a beach vacation.

Although each shade adapts to your complexion, I passed on this one because the limited color range wasn't a good fit for my olive undertones. Still, given the multiple rave reviews from our staff, it’s worth trying if you have the extra funds.

The world of sunscreen can sometimes feel like a catch-22: Either you're stuck using SPF that imparts a gnarly white cast, or you're using one that leaves your skin irritated and sensitive. The Supergoop! PLAY Everyday Lotion with SPF 50 sidesteps both of those issues, according to editorial assistant Katie Mogg. “The lightweight formula melts into my skin seamlessly, all while making it feel hydrated and nourished,” she says. Plus, it offers 80 minutes of water resistance, making it her go-to SPF for my sweaty outdoor running sessions.

Although I prefer a tinted face sunscreen, when I know I’ll be near the water or exercising outdoors I opt for this SPF. Play Everyday is my beach bag essential and for any trips to the park. It absorbs quickly without leaving behind a sticky residue on my body. Supergoop! doesn’t leave behind an ashy finish either. Instead, it blends flawlessly into my complexion.

The only thing I’d change about this sunscreen is the sizing options. There are four sizes, the most of any recommendations this list. However, only the extra large 18 fl. oz bottle comes with a pump. It would be nice to have the flexability of a pump with the other sizes, or at least the standard. But it’s not a true deal breaker, and I still like how slim the original squeeze bottle of sunscreen is and how it doesn’t take up too much space in my checked suitcase and beach bag.

Supergoop! is a favorite among dermatologists and our editors for its super-clear formulas—and rightfully so! This all-over version of the brand's star product—the Unseen Sunscreen SPF 40—does the same thing its predecessor does: it goes on invisible, feels velvety and weightless, and offers out-of-this-world sun protection.

"So many sunscreens have given my skin this heavy, greasy feeling right after I apply them, and on a really hot day in the sun, sometimes that can make you feel even hotter," says beauty contributor Danielle Jackson. "This formula is so light that I almost forgot I even had it on. It really makes you feel like you're not wearing anything."

Aloian has oily skin and easily breaks out, but she didn’t experience any body acne with this SPF. She didn't layer it with other body products, but she was impressed by how easily it spread, thanks to its more liquid texture, which blends into her sensitive areas like the neck. “I love this sunscreen—it doesn't leave any white streaks or irritate my skin. It'll definitely stay in my skincare routine for the long haul,” she says.

Honestly, the only con with this sunscreen is that it’s slightly pricey. However, we’ve been testing this SPF for over a month, and our editors predict each container will last them two to three months before a restock.

Ultraviolet radiation from the sun falls into two categories: ultraviolet A (UVA) and ultraviolet B (UVB). UVA rays cause signs of aging, such as hyperpigmentation, lines, and wrinkles. Meanwhile, UVB rays can cause more serious damage, including sunburn and skin cancer. Your safest bet is to only use broad-spectrum sunscreens to help protect against UVA and UVB rays.

Next, choose either a mineral or a chemical sunscreen. Here’s more insight to help you determine between the two formulations.

They both have benefits and limitations, but ultimately, the best one is the sunscreen you’ll actually use and reapply. As for me? Well, I like both types. However, I typically use mineral sunscreen on my face, so I can head outside immediately after work instead of lingering for the approximately 15-minute waiting period associated with chemical sunscreens.

Broad-spectrum coverage, sunscreen type, and SPF coverage are the big three considerations. But another factor worth emphasizing is other non-active skincare ingredients that will help bolster your complexion. Dermatologist Elyse Love, MD, is a big fan of niacinamide to calm the skin and improve its tone and texture. Also, look for ingredients that support your skin type and goals. For example, if you want to brighten your complexion, you'll look for a sunscreen with vitamin C. If you have dry skin, seek out hydrating ingredients like hyaluronic acid.

When we initially published this story in May 2019, it was a gallery featuring a handful of sunscreens. Nearly seven years later, we’ve seriously upgraded our product vetting process.

For starters, we polled dermatologists about the actual sunscreens they use IRL and recommend to patients. The doctors answered a series of questions about the efficacy, application, and real-world testing experience that helped inform their suggestions.

Next, I evaluated the hundreds of sunscreens in the Women’s Health beauty closet. I also polled Women’s Health and Men’s Health editors about their ride-or-die sunscreens. Our team varies across age, skin type, complexion, budget, and lifestyle. For example, fitness editor Cori Ritchey, CSCS, is a certified strength and conditioning coach and group fitness instructor. She has a no-frills approach to beauty and wants a simple sunscreen that delivers results, which she found in La Roche-Posay.

Clear sunscreens were carefully evaluated. Our team asked ourselves if the clear sunscreens squeezed out clear or were they white or creamy and then blended out without a trace? Associate health and fitness editor Addison Aloian and editorial assistant Katie Mogg found success with Supergoop!

Tinted sunscreens were also inspected because I know firsthand what it’s like to try and find your best color match only for it to look ruddy or cool in natural sunlight. With 17 flexible shades, Tower 28 delivers the most inclusive range among the sunscreens we vetted. The hues vary in depth and undertone, and offer light-to-medium coverage.

Whether you have oily, dry, or combination skin, there's something on our list for you. Meet our team’s all-time favorite sunscreens that we’ll continue to rely on throughout 2026.

You’ll want to keep an eye out for certain key phrases on the label. Dealing with sensitive skin? Dermatologist Marnie Nussbaum, MD, recommends fragrance-free and hypoallergenic formulas. She also prefers mineral sunscreens made with zinc oxide or titanium dioxide for sensitive skin because they’re less likely to cause irritation. Acne happens to the best of us, but your best path forward is to use an oil-free and non-comedogenic sunscreen that won’t congest your pores.

#4859. OpenAI's GPT 6.2 Astra Challenges Anthropic on Price, But Not Every Benchmark

OpenAI's GPT 6.2 Astra Challenges Anthropic on Price, But Not Every Benchmark

OpenAI launched GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol on Tuesday, updating its flagship and everyday AI models with better professional output, cheaper processing and stronger abilities to operate software on their own.

Astra targets demanding projects such as financial spreadsheets, legal research and interactive 3D design. Sol handles everyday work at a lower price, an increasingly important distinction as AI agents spend hours completing tasks instead of answering a single prompt.

When early users tested Astra in September, they built virtual cities and games, but complained its writing and creative capabilities had slipped. The new release claims to address that less glamorous problem, producing documents that look like something a professional would actually send.

Astra costs $8 per million input tokens and $40 per million output tokens through OpenAI's API, down 20% from the original model. Sol retains its $2 and $10 rates. Tokens are the chunks of text models process and generate, so fewer tokens can mean a smaller bill even when the listed rates stay the same.

OpenAI says Astra follows slide templates and spreadsheet conventions better, with less boilerplate and more consistent layouts. Those are company claims, not guarantees for every assignment.

Independent testing by Artificial Analysis puts Astra at 62 on its Intelligence Index, just a bit behind Anthropic's Claude Fable 5.2 at 65. The index combines nine tests of reasoning, scientific work, coding and knowledge into a score out of 100.

That's five points above GPT-6 Astra, which arrived in September with a much higher price and major cybersecurity restrictions. Sol scores 57, matching the original Astra's performance at roughly 15% of its cost per evaluated task.

Those mixed results follow Anthropic's Fable 5.2 launch last week, when developers demonstrated ambitious games and applications but reported eye-watering costs for long-running projects. Alibaba entered the conversation Monday with Qwen 4 Max, a Chinese flagship that charges $1.50 per million input tokens and $4.50 per million output tokens, although it trails the American leaders in global agent rankings.

OpenAI says Astra is its first externally released model to reach the High threshold for AI self-improvement, a safety classification measuring how much it can accelerate AI research. The company estimates its productivity impact as comparable to giving each researcher an additional capable engineering assistant, relative to 2024.

Both new models also meet OpenAI's Critical cybersecurity threshold. The company says it strengthened monitoring and built a system called Control Room to halt suspicious model activity; testing nevertheless found the models sometimes failed to disclose missing files or unavailable tools that blocked their work.

OpenAI says the models are available through ChatGPT Work and Codex for Plus, Pro, Enterprise and Edu users, and through the API for developers, but our GPT Plus subscription still doesn’t show those models, so this may be a slow rollout.

OpenAI has not yet added GPT-6.2 to its Daybreak program for vetted cybersecurity researchers.

#4858. The 9 Most Beautiful States in the US

The most beautiful states in the US prove just how shockingly diverse the country is: volcanic beaches, glacier-capped peaks, canyon-carved deserts, and misty rainforests define their landscapes. What people have built in those places is just as varied, from a royal palace in downtown Honolulu to Mary Colter’s stone watchtower on the rim of the Grand Canyon to the cedar-shingled studios of a modernist craft school on the coast of Maine. These nine states stand out on both counts, for the scenery that defines them and the architecture that holds its own against it. Keep in mind that no ranking can settle which state is most beautiful—they’re all worthy of a visit.

Hawaii is far from a monolithic state, with scenery changing from island to island. In Honolulu on Oahu, ʻIolani Palace, completed in 1882 for King Kalākaua, is the only royal palace on US soil—and it had electricity before the White House did.

Near Diamond Head, Doris Duke’s oceanfront estate, Shangri La, pairs 1930s modernism with architectural elements she brought from Morocco, Iran, Syria, and beyond. It’s now a museum of Islamic art, with tours departing from the Honolulu Museum of Art.

As for the natural landscape, Kauai, known as the Garden Isle, is home to the Nā Pali Coast, where green ridges drop sharply toward the Pacific. On Maui, Haleakalā’s broad volcanic summit often rises above a blanket of clouds. And on the Big Island, Hawaii Volcanoes National Park actively showcases the raw power of volcanoes—if you’re lucky, you might even catch an eruption.

Wyoming’s most famous photo moment might be the Teton Range rising abruptly above the sagebrush flats of Jackson Hole, ideally with one of Mormon Row’s weathered homestead barns in the foreground. Nearby, the tiny log Chapel of the Transfiguration, built in 1925, was sited so that the picture window behind its altar frames the peaks where stained glass would normally go.

In Yellowstone National Park, it’s all about color: Grand Prismatic Spring’s vivid rings stand out among the forested landscape, while the Grand Canyon of the Yellowstone exposes ochres and pinks in its steep walls. And steps from its namesake geyser, the Old Faithful Inn—designed by a 29-year-old Robert Reamer and opened in 1904—wraps a soaring lodgepole-pine lobby around a massive stone fireplace. It’s considered the largest log structure in the world.

Florida’s beaches are perhaps the state’s most scenic draw, but the architecture is just as distinctive. In 1979, Miami Beach’s Art Deco District, roughly a square mile of South Beach, became the nation’s first urban 20th-century historic district on the National Register, with more than 800 buildings listed. Across Biscayne Bay, industrialist James Deering’s Vizcaya, a villa completed in 1916, faces the water with formal gardens by Diego Suarez. Addison Mizner gave Palm Beach its Mediterranean Revival look; his Via Mizner, a winding pedestrian lane off Worth Avenue built in 1923, survives today.

St. Augustine, founded by the Spanish in 1565, pairs the coquina-stone Castillo de San Marcos with Henry Flagler’s Hotel Ponce de Leon, a Spanish Renaissance–style palace from 1888 that’s now Flagler College. Architecture buffs should detour to Lakeland, where Frank Lloyd Wright’s campus for Florida Southern College is the largest single-site collection of his architecture in the world. And on the Gulf Coast, Sarasota’s midcentury modernists adapted the International Style to the subtropics, most famously in Paul Rudolph’s 1953 Umbrella House.

On Maine’s coast, Acadia National Park packs a surprising amount of scenery into a small area: granite headlands, spruce forest, offshore islands, and views of the Atlantic. Look closely, and you'll notice the park’s impressive stonework, too. John D. Rockefeller Jr. financed its network of carriage roads, built between 1913 and 1940, along with 16 of the 17 stone-faced bridges that carry them over streams and gorges—no two are alike.

Don’t forget the coastal villages, from ever-popular Bar Harbor and its shingle-style and Queen Anne houses to Stonington, a working fishing town on Deer Isle. Elsewhere on Deer Isle, Edward Larrabee Barnes’s 1961 campus for the Haystack Mountain School of Crafts, an underrated masterpiece of American modernism, steps down a granite slope toward Jericho Bay, its cedar-shingled cabins and studios linked by boardwalks.

California has a little of everything, from the architectural hubs of Los Angeles and San Francisco to breathtaking natural settings. In Yosemite, El Capitan and Half Dome are jaw-dropping from the valley floor, but even more so from the top for those daring enough to make the climb. Back down in the valley, the Ahwahnee hotel, which opened in 1927, appears to be built of granite and redwood—but the “wood” is actually fireproof concrete, poured into molds and stained to look like timber. In the desert, Palm Springs is a showcase of midcentury modernism, with Richard Neutra’s 1946 Kaufmann House as its best-known example.

But the California coast is undeniably the state’s most famous landscape, and the 656 miles of Highway 1 deliver architecture along with the views. Above San Simeon, Hearst Castle, which Julia Morgan designed for William Randolph Hearst over nearly three decades, crowns a hilltop overlooking the Pacific. Continue north past the bluffs of Big Sur and storybook Carmel-by-the-Sea to the Sonoma Coast, where the redwood-clad buildings of the Sea Ranch, a planned community begun in the mid-1960s, are tucked into hedgerows to leave the meadows and bluffs open.

New York State’s famous architecture isn’t limited to the Manhattan skyline—though the city certainly pulls its weight on the architecture front. In the Adirondacks, wooded mountains surround lakes such as Lake Placid and the three Saranac Lakes. The “great camps” that wealthy families began building along their shores in the Gilded Age turned the log cabin into high style. You can still stay in one: The Point, on Upper Saranac Lake, was built in the early 1930s as Camp Wonundra for William Avery Rockefeller II and is now an 11-room Relais & Châteaux hotel, the first in North America.

In the Hudson Valley, painter Frederic Church’s hilltop villa, Olana, features a design style he called “Persian, adapted to the Occident.” The Finger Lakes offer a gentler landscape of long, narrow lakes bordered by vineyards and small towns, plus the gorge at Watkins Glen State Park, where a stone path meanders past tumbling cascades and swirling pools. And in Buffalo, you’ll find Frank Lloyd Wright’s Darwin D. Martin House, one of his finest Prairie-style designs.

The Grand Canyon is a tough act to follow, but on its South Rim, architect Mary Colter spent decades designing buildings meant to hold their own beside it. Her Hopi House, which opened in 1905, is a multistory stone building shaped like a Hopi pueblo; her Desert View Watchtower, completed in 1932, is a 70-foot stone tower modeled on Ancestral Puebloan structures, with a Snake Legend mural inside by Hopi artist Fred Kabotie.

Sedona’s red-rock buttes are spectacular on their own, but the Chapel of the Holy Cross, a modernist concrete chapel built directly into a pair of sandstone buttes and completed in 1956, gives them a focal point. North of Phoenix, Paolo Soleri’s Arcosanti, an experimental desert town of concrete domes and arches begun in 1970, is still a work in progress. And in Scottsdale, in the foothills of the McDowell Mountains, Frank Lloyd Wright’s Taliesin West—his winter home and studio from 1937 until his death in 1959—is now a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

Texas’s landscapes range from the Chihuahuan Desert to the Gulf Coast to the bayous of Caddo Lake. In Big Bend National Park, the Chisos Mountains rise above dry plains, and the Rio Grande cuts through the narrow walls of Santa Elena Canyon. In Marfa, minimalist artist Donald Judd turned a former army post into the Chinati Foundation, a museum built around permanent, large-scale installations, including his 100 mill-aluminum boxes lined up inside two converted artillery sheds.

In Fort Worth, Louis Kahn’s Kimbell Art Museum, completed in 1972, draws architects from around the world to see natural light wash down its concrete cycloid vaults; Tadao Ando’s Modern Art Museum of Fort Worth sits just across the street. Central Texas has rolling hills, and in spring, bluebonnets and Indian paintbrush color the roadsides around Fredericksburg, a town with German heritage.

Mount Rainier is perhaps Washington’s most familiar landmark, its glaciers and snowfields visible above forests and summer wildflower meadows. The North Cascades offer even more peaks, with jagged ridges rising above turquoise Diablo Lake, while the trails in Olympic National Park lead through mossy rainforest and out to driftwood-strewn beaches.

Seattle holds its own against all that scenery. Downtown, the Central Library—designed by Rem Koolhaas’s OMA with local firm LMN and opened in 2004—wraps its stacked floors in a faceted net of glass and steel, while the Space Needle, built for the 1962 World’s Fair, remains the skyline’s signature. Outside Seattle, Port Townsend’s Victorian storefronts overlook the water, and in the Walla Walla Valley, vineyard rows and wheat fields spread across rolling hills, with the Blue Mountains rising beyond them.

#4857. Maple Finance CEO targets up to $15B in assets by the end of 2027

Sidney Powell aims to reach $15 billion in assets under management by the end of 2027 as the firm looks to expand into tokenized lending and traditional finance.

Onchain asset manager Maple Finance is aiming to grow its assets under management (AUM) to between $10 billion and $15 billion by the end of 2027 as it looks to attract more traditional financial (TradFi) firms, according to CEO Sidney Powell.

In an exclusive interview with Cointelegraph on Monday, Powell said the company is also targeting a loan book of around $4.5 billion to $5 billion.

The plans come as Maple looks to grow beyond lending backed primarily by cryptocurrencies such as Bitcoin (BTC) and attract more traditional financial firms, with Powell expecting tokenized assets and stablecoins to play a major role in the company’s growth.

Maple reported $4.7 billion in AUM at the end of the third quarter, up 18% from a year earlier. However, Maple’s dashboard showed around $3.9 billion in AUM on Tuesday.

Outstanding loans rose 12% from a year earlier to $1.7 billion, while quarterly revenue increased 5% to $4.4 million, bringing annualized revenue to $17.6 million. Still, outstanding loans fell 9% from the previous quarter, while quarterly revenue remained flat.

Tokenized assets are digital versions of traditional assets, such as stocks and bonds, that can be held and traded on a blockchain. Separately, stablecoins are digital tokens designed to maintain a stable value relative to a reference asset, most commonly a currency such as the US dollar.

The market for tokenized real-world assets has grown significantly over the past year, with their value on public blockchains reaching about $39.9 billion as of Nov. 11, up 52% year-over-year, according to RWA.xyz. The value of tokenized stocks alone rose from about $678 million in January to nearly $3.9 billion in November.

Maple assets under management. Source: Maple Finance

Powell expects tokenized stocks to grow fivefold to tenfold in 2027, which could allow Maple to offer loans backed by tokenized shares rather than relying mainly on cryptocurrency collateral.

“I think tokenized equities are going to be really big,” he said. “You’ll start to see more tokenized equity lending.”

Under this model, borrowers could use tokenized stocks as collateral to obtain loans without having to sell their investments, similar to how Bitcoin-backed lending works today.

“Ultimately, that’s really positive for the space because it gives you tokenized assets to lend against that are not correlated with Bitcoin,” Powell said. Bitcoin is the largest cryptocurrency with a market capitalization of over $1.28 trillion as of Nov. 17.

Maple is also discussing credit facilities through which banks would finance its Bitcoin-backed lending, Powell said.

“At the moment, we’re looking at a first deal where we’re speaking with banks about warehouse facilities for the Bitcoin-backed lending, so they would be a funder to us,” Powell said.

Maple already provides financing for a warehouse facility supporting Kraken’s crypto-backed lending program, which was announced in June. The proposed bank arrangements would instead bring funding into Maple’s lending business.

Powell added that Maple could pursue separate deals with US banks and lenders involving loans originated by TradFi institutions and subsequently brought onto blockchain networks. “I think that’s going to be a big market for 2027,” he said.

Maple outlined plans in September to lend against portfolios of asset-backed and mortgage-backed securities and finance loans originated by fintech companies. It said at the time that each new strategy would initially be capped at 5% of its overall deposit base.

Another priority is expanding partnerships with financial technology companies and digital banks that want to offer customers ways to earn interest on their stablecoin holdings. Powell said Maple is already in discussions with several large firms about potential products, with announcements possible in the first quarter of 2027.

“My view is that’s the kind of path Maple has to go down in order to grow, and we have to focus more on these larger institutional allocators,” Powell said. “That’s ultimately where most of the balance sheet is in traditional finance.”

That approach to expansion is also at the center of a leadership disagreement, according to Powell.

Related: Arch Lending eyes tokenized stocks as next collateral market

Maple’s growth plans come amid a leadership shakeup after co-founder and executive chairman Joe Flanagan and chief operating officer Ryan O’Shea announced plans last week to leave over disagreements about the company’s future direction.

Flanagan said his differences with Powell involved strategy and leadership, while O’Shea said he had reached a different view on the direction Maple should take.

Powell said the differences centered on how best to expand the business, particularly as TradFi institutions become more involved in crypto lending.

“We had a difference of opinion on the best way to scale things,” he told Cointelegraph. “This year, I think, more than ever, we started to see that real convergence with traditional finance, fintechs and neobanks. And my view is that that is kind of the right path for us to scale.”

The planned departures prompted questions from Maple’s investors, partners and clients, some of whom contacted Powell seeking clarification. Powell said the departures were unrelated to problems with Maple’s loan book or the health of the business.

“The important thing is conveying to them and reassuring them that this wasn’t to do with any issues in Maple’s loan book or any issues with the business,” Powell said. “It is just a difference on what is the best pathway to scale Maple from here.”

Maple Finance’s native token, SYRUP is currently trading at $0.103 as of 6:50 pm UTC on Tuesday, with a market capitalization of $123 million, according to CoinMarketCap. The token is down about 46% over the past 30 days and 74% over the past year.

#4856. The 8 Best Slippers for Women for Max Coziness, Tested By a Style Writer

From couch-rotting to errands, these kicks have you covered.

Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

Now that the weather has cooled down and leaves are on the ground, my style writer brain is in peak outfit mode. I’ve already imagined the ways I’ll wear my leather jackets, chunky knits, and bootcut jeans. But before I start styling my way through the fall and winter, there’s one essential I always reach for first: slippers. I test a lot of shoes in the name of journalism, and few spark more joy than a pair of cute slippers that add the perfect cozy feel to any outfit. Whether I’m channeling my inner couch potato on a lazy Sunday or running errands around town, the best slippers in my stash hit the sweet spot of soft, supportive, and actually stylish.

A lot of the same principles that apply to shopping for supportive sneakers also apply to slippers, says Anne Sharkey, DPM, a podiatrist at Solely Podiatry in Austin, TX. After all, a slipper is the ultimate cozy shoe, but it’s also incredibly useful for keeping your arches happy while walking around hardwood floors at home. That’s why Sharkey says cushioning and arch support are key. Your slippers should feel plush underfoot, but not so squishy that you lose stability. Where you plan to wear them also matters: A pair of house slippers needs less traction and durability than a pair for outdoors, which should have a thicker, more grippy bottom.

After over a year of testing, I found slippers that are plush enough to lounge in, supportive enough for a spin around town, and stylish enough that you’ll actually want to wear them.

When it comes to a slipper that checks every box (plush, supportive, and legitimately stylish), the Ugg Cozy Slipper is the one I always come back to. I’ve been wearing this slipper since fall 2024 with everything from jeans and Henleys to matching sweat sets.

The slipper earns its name with extra-cozy materials, from the sheepskin fur lining to the sweater-knit outer and fluffy collar. I love that it keeps my feet warm and toasty, even during cold winter months. Board-certified foot and ankle surgeon Bobby Pourizaee, DPM says this slipper is excellent for comfort and lounging. Podiatrist and board-certified foot and ankle surgeon Bruce Pinker, DPM agrees, adding that the slip-on style makes this slipper easy to wear.

Beneath the fluff, there’s real structure that keeps my feet fatigue-free. The contoured footbed and firm-yet-plush midsole made with 17 mm of sheepskin hug my arches just right. The outsole is sturdy and grippy, made with dense EVA foam and tons of traction. I wear it on long walks with my dog around the Long Island suburbs and never worry about slipping or falling, no matter the weather. However, it’s still lightweight enough to feel like an indoor slipper.

Pinker says that it could be improved if the heel region were closed for more support and stability, but the easy-on, easy-off fit is part of why I love this slipper. If you’re after something warm, cozy, and super stylish for both indoor and outdoor wear, I can’t recommend this slipper enough.

For a cozy, budget-friendly slipper that doesn’t skimp on comfort, the Dearfoams Lacey Memory Foam Slipper is the one I’ve been living in lately. At under $30, this slipper is way more cushy, warm, and supportive than lots of other house slippers I’ve worn.

I padded around my house in this slipper nonstop for about a year, and it held up beautifully through coffee runs to the kitchen, long hours at my desk, and quick trips to grab packages. It’s definitely a house slipper, but in the best way possible—pure comfort, with just enough structure to feel supportive.

The memory foam cushioning is what makes this slipper so comfortable, Sharkey says. Each step in it feels super plush, molding to the shape of my foot for that “walking on pillows” feel. The fleece lining also keeps my feet cozy without overheating, and the soft knit upper gives it a lounge-all-day kind of vibe that pairs perfectly with pajamas and sweatpants. I absolutely love the heel and arch cushioning, especially when my feet ache after a long day commuting to and from Manhattan, but Sharkey says they should only be worn in the house since they lack the structure needed for long periods on your feet.

But for a house slipper, there’s way more support than I expected. The raised heel area keeps the slipper from sliding off my foot, even when I’m walking up or down stairs. It’s a small but thoughtful feature that makes it feel a bit more secure than your average slip-on. And while the outsole isn’t meant for outdoor adventures, it’s durable enough for quick steps onto the porch or grabbing the mail.

I wore this slipper for nearly a year straight while trodding around my house, and absolutely love them. However, I will say that at about the 10-month mark, they needed to be replaced, as they stretched out a bit and lost some of the much-needed cushioning, support, and traction.

Thanks to its incredible level of cushioning, the Vionic Gemma II Mule Slipper keeps my feet pain-free even after walking in it all day. Pourizaee says it's a strong recommendation thanks to the contoured footbed. The midsole is made from a flexible EVA foam that not only feels super plush under my foot but is designed to absorb shock and reduce stress on the joints. I have lingering ankle and foot pain on one side from a previous high ankle sprain, and while some shoes exacerbate those symptoms, this slipper keeps my feet happy. That comes as no surprise, since this slipper earned an APMA Seal of Acceptance.

It also has great support and stability features. Pinker says it would be improved with a closed-heel design, but I find that the deep heel cup helps, and the strap closure keeps my foot firmly planted—even while speed walking on city sidewalks. Pourizaee adds that the contoured footbed helps keep feet aligned and relieves foot strain. While I often wake up with sore feet that hurt as soon as I step out of bed, I find that when I’ve worn this slipper the day before, foot fatigue is next to zero.

If you like a cozy slipper, the Gemma II delivers. I have the cream color, which is made with a wool upper that keeps my feet warm and looks cute with all my cold-weather loungewear. Other styles have a faux-fur or flannel upper, which also looks super warm and cozy. Plus, since the slipper is designed for indoor and outdoor wear, the synthetic outsole is ultra-durable with a patterned tread design. I’ve even gone for post-rain walks with my dog on wet pavement, and never felt like I was going to slip.

Overall, this slipper is warm, cozy, and ultra-cushioned. It keeps my feet happy with the plush feel underfoot, and I love keeping it by the door when I need a cute shoe to slip on fast.

If you need a slipper with serious arch support, the Orthofeet Charlotte Slipper delivers. Plus, it comes with additional insoles and spacers for days when my feet need extra support.

The ergonomic sole not only has ample cushioning underfoot, but also the subtle “rocker” design, which refers to a little lift under the heel and toe so those two parts of the shoe don’t touch the ground when standing still, similar to a rocking chair. That shape propels you forward with each step and also helps take some pressure off the joints. Plus, the EVA outsole also has lots of traction patterns to keep every step feeling stable and secure.

I also love the faux fur lining and insole that feels super cozy and keeps my feet warm even while walking outdoors on chilly mornings. The suede outer adds to that cozy vibe and looks super cute. I initially wasn’t sure if this slipper would be my style, but I find myself reaching for it all the time when I leave the house for quick errands and coffee dates with friends. I have the taupe color and often pair it with ankle jeans and sweaters for a comfortable fall fit.

While it does run slightly small, the brand offers half sizes, and the slipper comes with customizable features, so I didn’t find it an issue at all. However, if you’re concerned about fit, I recommend ordering a half size down.

That contouring feature does wonders for making sure the slipper stays on, even while trekking all around town. However, Sharkey says the backless design does tend to slip off the feet if you’re not careful. I haven’t had any issues there, but it’s something to keep in mind if your feet need an ultra-supportive shoe—in which case, the Orthofeet Charlotte Slipper might be a better choice.

The rubber outsole gives this slip-on shoe a major upgrade, since it helps provide traction when I wear it outside. I keep this slipper mainly for wearing around the house or quick errands, but I have worn it during short, casual walks without worry. The fluffy sherpa material, inside and out, makes it a super cozy option for lazy days cuddled up on the couch and keeps my feet warm even when I take it for a spin outdoors.

Plus, there’s plenty of chic color options. I went with the cream, which I find pairs well with almost anything in my closet—but there’s also a black and brown for additional neutrals, and a dusty purple or tomato red option for something more bold. While this slipper from Bombas might not be the most supportive option, I’d recommend it to anyone looking for a plush, super stylish slipper.

Clogs get a bad rap for making your feet sweat, slide around, and (sorry!) being kind of ugly. But this slip-on clog from Rothy’s nails it on the style front, and is also durable, breathable, and super comfortable. The Casual Clog is well-loved by me and executive editor Abigail Cuffey—oh, and Sharkey recommends it, too.

This slipper/clog hybrid is made with the brand’s signature cushioning made from recycled water bottles and arch support that Sharkey says is ultra comfortable. She also says she likes that the heel cup is a bit deeper than your standard slipper, which helps with stability. I find that the deep heel cup helps cover the back of my foot, so it doesn’t slip off when I’m running around the house doing laundry or walking up and down stairs. The outsole is also made from recycled water bottles and has a grooved design that makes it super durable with tons of traction. I usually wear it for casual outings and meeting up with friends, and find it looks great with baggy jeans and sweaters for a casual-yet-put-together look.

While I own the merino wool version, Cuffey owns both the merino wool and hemp styles. She’s been wearing the hemp clog since fall 2024, and loves that the ultra-cushioned footbed molds to her feet. “It feels like a hug for your heels and toes,” she says. She wears it as a lounge shoe and an outdoor shoe, because of the grippy outsole and substantial feel. Cuffey’s thoughts on the merino wool clog are generally the same, but she loves that the wool feels a little cozier while still airy and breathable. “I usually go through slippers so fast because they get so gross, but Rothy’s Casual Clogs are the first ones that have staying power in my closet,” she says.

It does run a little wide, but the fabric is stretchy, so I haven’t had any issues with it feeling too loose on my feet. But if you’re in between sizes, Rothy’s recommends sizing down for a better fit.

#4855. Jensen Huang’s Houses: Exploring the Former Nvidia CEO’s $38 Million San Francisco Mansion and Other Properties

It’s been a big week for Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang. The billionaire announced he is stepping down as CEO of the AI hardware giant following reports that he had at least two extramarital affairs: one with a suspected Chinese spy, and another with one of his company’s senior executives (other reports allege a third affair with another Nvidia employee). Huang will reportedly testify before Congress later this month to discuss his relationship with the alleged spy. We can only assume that the Taipei City native is weathering the storm at home, but where are Jensen Huang’s houses? Even Huang himself may be wondering about the answer to that question, if a recent New York Times interview is any indication (more on that later).

Unsurprisingly, the tech titan hasn’t strayed too far from Silicon Valley, where Nvidia has been based since it was founded in the mid-’80s, with his real estate purchases. After graduating from Oregon State University, where he met his wife, Lori Huang, Huang began buying properties in California’s Bay Area, and he and Lori still own two of them. So far, the superbillionaire’s only exception to that rule has been an estate on Maui in Hawaii. Time will tell if the scandal spurs any real estate changes for him.

One thing that will presumably change about Huang’s home life in the immediate future: footing the bill for his security team. Nvidia has, until now, covered the cost of its former CEO’s private security. The company spent about $4 million in 2026 on “home security, protection during personal travel, consulting, and drivers” for Huang, per the New York Post. Though that arrangement is likely coming to an end, that shouldn’t be too big a problem for Jensen; the scandal has put Nvidia’s stock—and therefore Jensen’s net worth—in a slight flux, but he is still worth an estimated $144.7 billion at the time of publication.

Read on for a rundown of Jensen Huang’s houses dating back to his arrival in Silicon Valley.

According to The New York Times, Huang married Lori shortly after his 1984 graduation from Oregon State University, where they met as lab partners in an electrical engineering class. The newlywed graduates hightailed it to Silicon Valley to start their careers as microchip designers, and Jensen bought his first house: a 1,500-square-foot three-bedroom home in San Jose, California. It’s unclear exactly when or for how much he bought the property, but Jensen sold it in 1988 for $185,000.

That same year, Huang and Lori moved into a larger San Jose home that they bought for $338,000. With 2,300 square feet of interior living space, it had four bedrooms. Huang lived here when he co-founded Nvidia in 1993; he sold the house in 2002 for $500,000, the Wall Street Journal reports.

From there, the Huangs moved into an even more upgraded residence: a 7,000-square-foot home in Los Altos Hills, a tony area about 15 miles from the Nvidia headquarters. They paid $6.9 million for the newly built six-bedroom dwelling in 2003. According to Realtor.com, the two-story house hosts a resort-worthy swimming pool. The Huangs still own this house.

A year after buying his house in Los Altos Hills, Huang paid $7.5 million for a Hawaiian estate. The oceanfront property is located within Wailea Resort, an exclusive gated community on the south side of Maui, per the Wall Street Journal. The contemporary-style mansion reportedly has seven bedrooms across about 8,000 square feet. The Huangs still maintain this residence too.

In 2017, Huang made his most recent real estate purchase: a newly completed $38 million mansion in the high-end Pacific Heights neighborhood on San Francisco’s Gold Coast. The residence is modern in style, with a curved roofline and a limestone exterior. It boasts 11,400 square feet of interior living space, with seven bedrooms, seven full bathrooms, three half-baths, a wine cellar, an outdoor kitchen, an elevator, a home theater, a gym with a sauna, a library, numerous fireplaces, and a fifth-floor observation deck with views of the Golden Gate Bridge. The house took four years to construct, its developer told the WSJ.

San Francisco’s famous Golden Gate Bridge.

This seems to be Huang’s primary residence—although, according to a September 2026 New York Times interview, he could not tell you where it is. “There are a lot of skills that don’t matter,” Huang told the outlet in response to a question about AI weakening students’ basic math skills. “My first confession, I actually don’t know my address.… One day I had to pump gas—it was a few years ago. They needed my ZIP code, and I panicked. I didn’t know my ZIP code. I don’t know my telephone number. I forget these things. I can live with it.”

#4853. Nvidia Shares Rise After Earnings Beat in First Report Since Jensen Huang's Exit

Nvidia Shares Rise After Earnings Beat in First Report Since Jensen Huang's Exit

Nvidia shares climbed roughly 2% in after-hours trading Tuesday after the AI chipmaker delivered another record quarter, beating Wall Street expectations on revenue and earnings while forecasting stronger-than-expected sales for the current period.

The results offered some relief to investors after a brutal selloff that wiped hundreds of billions of dollars from Nvidia's market value following the resignation of co-founder Jensen Huang.

According to Nvidia's earnings release, revenue reached $115.8 billion for the fiscal third quarter ended October 25, up 103% from a year earlier and comfortably above analysts' expectations of approximately $109.1 billion.

Adjusted earnings per share came in at $2.68, beating the roughly $2.47 consensus estimate. Net income under generally accepted accounting principles reached $65.3 billion, more than double the $31.9 billion reported a year earlier.

Nvidia's data center division generated $107.6 billion in revenue, up 110% year over year and accounting for approximately 93% of total sales. The company also confirmed that its Vera Rubin NVL72 computing platform has begun shipping, extending the hardware roadmap that helped make Nvidia the dominant supplier of AI processors.

The company expects fourth-quarter revenue of $130 billion, plus or minus 3%, compared with Wall Street estimates of approximately $125.3 billion, per Reuters. That forecast includes an additional week in the reporting period and assumes no data center computing revenue from China.

Tuesday's report marks Nvidia's first financial results since Huang resigned November 12, ending his 33-year tenure following revelations of extramarital affairs involving company employees and a businesswoman suspected by U.S. intelligence officials of having ties to China. Those intelligence allegations remain unproven, and an independent investigation is ongoing.

To add more drama to the story, the Securities and Exchange Commission opened a civil investigation into whether Nvidia violated investor-disclosure laws.

Colette Kress, Nvidia's longtime chief financial officer and interim CEO, sought to reassure investors about the company's future. "Our momentum is real," she said in the earnings announcement, adding that the Vera Rubin rollout was off to a strong start and the product roadmap remained on track.

Huang said Tuesday that he would be honored to return as CEO if the board believed it was in Nvidia's best interests. His statement followed public support from Elon Musk and President Donald Trump, although the board is not considering reinstatement and continues searching for a permanent replacement.

Nvidia's fundamentals look considerably better than its stock chart. Despite Tuesday's rebound, shares remain roughly 35% below their October peak near $240, and the technical indicators suggest sellers still control the broader trend.

The daily chart shows immediate support around $150, close to the $148.80 low reached during last week's selloff. A decisive break below that area could expose further downside, while a sustained recovery would first need to reclaim resistance around $164.40 to $165.60.

That former support area has become resistance following the breakdown, as Decrypt's earlier technical analysis identified. Above it, the chart shows additional hurdles near $176 and between $184 and $189, making a return to the previous trading range far from automatic.

The Relative Strength Index, or RSI, is around 22.5 on the supplied daily chart, well below the conventional oversold threshold of 30. That makes a short-term rebound plausible, but oversold readings are not proof that a bottom has formed.

The Average Directional Index, or ADX, sits near 45.4, indicating a strong prevailing trend, with directional signals favoring sellers. The faster exponential moving average remains above the slower one, a positive longer-term configuration that has not prevented the recent collapse.

Tuesday's earnings beat gives bulls a potential catalyst, but the after-hours bounce has yet to reclaim the chart's first major resistance around $164.40. Kress is scheduled to lead the company's 5 p.m. Eastern earnings call, the first without Huang, as investors look for answers about Nvidia's leadership and its next phase of growth.

#4852. CFTC halts some Kalshi Trump mention markets over manipulation concerns

The CFTC stayed Kalshi’s Trump-related mention markets after raising concerns about manipulation risks, giving the platform until Dec. 11 to defend its contracts.

The US Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) has ordered a temporary halt to certain Kalshi prediction markets allowing traders to bet on words or phrases US President Donald Trump might say, citing concerns about potential manipulation.

In a Nov. 13 order, the CFTC targeted Kalshi’s “What nicknames will Trump say before 2027?” market and its TRUMPSAY contract series. The regulator said Kalshi had listed the nickname market after a Sept. 22 staff advisory warning of manipulation risks without updating its certification to address those concerns.

The CFTC confirmed to Cointelegraph that it had stayed the listing of certain Kalshi mention markets pending further proceedings. Kalshi has until Dec. 11 to respond, and the regulator has not made a final determination on whether the contracts comply with federal law.

“We disagree with this decision,” Kalshi CEO Tarek Mansour told Axios on Tuesday. He argued that markets predicting Trump’s words have economic value because the president’s remarks can move financial markets.

In its September advisory, CFTC staff warned that people whose actions determine a contract’s outcome, or those close to them, could influence the result or exploit advance knowledge of it.

Kalshi had previously stopped listing numerous other mention markets at the regulator’s request, including all sports-related mention contracts, Reuters reported, citing a person familiar with the matter.

Related: Kalshi ends Donald Trump Jr. advisory role over Polymarket investment: Reuters

The regulatory action follows an earlier insider-trading case involving Gabriel Perez, a former White House teleprompter operator who used advance knowledge of President Trump’s speeches to profit from Kalshi contracts, according to the CFTC.

In July, Cointelegraph reported that Kalshi’s surveillance system had flagged Perez’s trades and referred them to the CFTC. The regulator’s subsequent Aug. 28 enforcement order found that Perez generally had access to Trump’s prepared speeches about an hour before delivery and used the information to bet on whether specific words would be spoken. He profited on 39 of 43 contracts across 14 mention markets and, on one occasion, changed his position after Trump skipped or deviated from part of a prepared speech.

In August, the CFTC ordered Perez to return $107,539 in profits and pay a $65,000 civil penalty for trading on nonpublic information. Perez settled without admitting the agency’s findings.
